points: **s.97F:** the MA can raise an individual bank's minimums under the Banking Ordinance, after giving it a chance to make representations.
**Binding add-on:** This is how the Pillar 2A add-on from the supervisory review under SPM CA-G-5 becomes legally binding.
deepDive.takeaway: The bank's real floor is therefore higher than the published Basel figures, and it is usually confidential.

deepDive.heading: Basel III final reform
points: **What took effect:** Most of the Basel III final reform package took effect on 1 January 2025: revised credit and operational risk, and an [[output floor]] that rises in stages to 72.5%.
**Separate timetable:** The market risk and CVA changes followed their own HKMA timetable, so confirm which apply to the bank.
**Standardised approaches:** For a bank on standardised approaches the floor rarely bites.
**What matters more:** The revised risk weights and the new operational risk charge matter more.

deepDive.heading: Liquidity and large exposures
deepDive.lede: Liquidity uses two tiers.
points: **Category 1:** institutions designated by the MA; they must meet the LCR and NSFR.
**Category 2:** all other AIs, which must meet a 25% [[LMR]]; category 2A institutions must also meet a 75% core funding ratio.
**Exposure limits:** the Exposure Limits Rules cap exposure to any counterparty group at 25% of Tier 1.
**Connected parties:** They also govern exposures to connected parties, including the bank's own shareholders.

items.label: Category 1
items.note: Institutions designated by the MA

items.label: Category 2
items.note: All other AIs; category 2A also a 75% core funding ratio

items.label: Large exposures
items.note: Cap on exposure to any counterparty group

deepDive.heading: Loss-making digital banks
deepDive.lede: For a loss-making digital bank, the key judgements concern runway.

visual.caption: For a loss-making digital bank, the key judgements concern runway.

items.label: Operating losses
items.note: Plus deductions for tax-loss deferred tax assets and capitalised software

items.label: CET1 capital
items.note: Accounting equity overstates it

items.label: Board's internal trigger
items.note: Set above the Pillar 2A floor plus buffers
items.rel: the capital plan shows when ratios reach

points: **Operating losses:** Operating losses reduce CET1 directly.
**Deductions:** deferred tax assets arising from tax losses are deducted, and so is capitalised software held as an intangible, so accounting equity overstates regulatory capital.
**Capital plan:** it should show when ratios will reach the board's internal trigger, which sits above the Pillar 2A floor plus buffers.
**Parent injections:** these should be approved in advance and documented.
**Dividends:** not an option until accumulated losses have been cleared, because company law allows distributions only out of distributable profits (Cap. 622, Part 6).

provisions.ref: Capital adequacy ratios, buffers and leverage ratio
provisions.title: Minimum capital ratios and buffers
provisions.summary: The Rules set the minimum CET1 (4.5%), Tier 1 (6%) and total capital (8%) ratios and define what counts as capital and which deductions apply. They also set the capital conservation, countercyclical and D-SIB buffers, which carry distribution constraints, and a minimum leverage ratio of 3%.
provisions.counselNote: The legal definition of eligible capital decides whether a parent injection counts as CET1. Distribution constraints also limit dividends and discretionary bonuses before any formal breach.

provisions.title: MA's power to vary capital requirements for a particular AI
provisions.summary: Allows the MA to vary capital requirement rules for a particular AI, including raising its minimum capital adequacy ratios, where it is satisfied on reasonable grounds that this is prudent. The AI may make representations before the variation takes effect.
provisions.counselNote: This is the legal route for Pillar 2A add-ons. Treat a proposed variation as a decision with due-process rights, and keep the resulting minimums in a controlled, confidential register.

provisions.title: Basel III final reform package
provisions.summary: Amends Cap. 155L to implement the revised credit risk, operational risk, market risk (FRTB) and CVA risk frameworks and the output floor. Following LegCo negative vetting in early 2024, a commencement notice gazetted in October 2024 brought them into force on 1 January 2025. The HKMA set a separate timetable for the market risk and CVA requirements; confirm which are in force for the bank.
provisions.counselNote: Any capital plan, board paper or pricing model from before 2025 rests on the old risk weights. Ask Finance to confirm that projections and RWA engines reflect the amended Rules.

provisions.title: Liquidity ratios
provisions.summary: Category 1 institutions, designated by the MA, must keep the LCR and NSFR at or above 100%. Category 2 institutions must meet a 25% Liquidity Maintenance Ratio, and category 2A institutions must also meet a 75% Core Funding Ratio. SPM LM-1 gives the detailed supervisory guidance.
provisions.counselNote: Confirm the bank's designated category in writing. Treat a ratio breach as a notification event with an escalation path to the board and the HKMA.

provisions.title: Large exposure limit and connected exposures
provisions.summary: Limits an AI's exposure to any single counterparty or linked counterparty group to 25% of Tier 1 capital, and separately controls exposures to connected parties. The Rules came into force on 1 July 2019 and took full effect after a six-month grace period. SPM CR-G-8 treats exposures at or above 10% of Tier 1 as large exposures.
provisions.counselNote: Intra-group placements, guarantees and service prepayments to the parent are exposures to connected parties, so check them before signing. Placing surplus deposits with a few banks can also reach the 25% limit.

provisions.title: Public regulatory disclosures
provisions.summary: Requires AIs to publish standardised information on capital, RWA, leverage, liquidity and risk management, using HKMA templates and at prescribed frequencies.
provisions.counselNote: Pillar 3 disclosures are public statements. They need the same verification and sign-off discipline as financial statements, and must be consistent with what the bank tells investors and customers.

provisions.title: Supervisory review process (Pillar 2)
provisions.summary: A statutory guideline issued under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance. It sets out how the HKMA assesses each AI's capital adequacy assessment process (CAAP/ICAAP) and sets Pillar 2 requirements, including expectations on stress testing within the CAAP.
provisions.counselNote: The ICAAP is a board document. Make sure the board can show it challenged the document rather than simply receiving it.

provisions.title: Stress-testing
provisions.summary: A guidance note, revised in 2012 to reflect Basel stress-testing principles, on how AIs should design, govern and use stress tests. The HKMA applies it proportionately to the scale and complexity of the AI.
provisions.counselNote: Stress-test outputs feed capital planning, recovery triggers and exit-plan triggers. Make sure the scenarios include a fast digital deposit run and a failure of parent support.

provisions.title: Interest rate risk in the banking book
provisions.summary: Sets out HKMA expectations for measuring, managing and reporting interest rate risk on non-trading positions, broadly in line with the Basel IRRBB standards.
provisions.counselNote: A bank that wins deposits by pricing promotions and then holds fixed-rate assets is exposed to interest rate risk. Product terms on repricing and early withdrawal are legal levers that affect this risk.

provisions.title: Limits on distributions inside the buffers
provisions.summary: When a bank's CET1 ratio falls into its buffer range (capital conservation, countercyclical and any D-SIB buffer), the Rules cap distributions such as dividends, discretionary bonuses and AT1 coupons at a maximum distributable amount until the buffers are rebuilt.
provisions.counselNote: Separately, company law allows dividends only out of distributable profits (Companies Ordinance, Cap. 622, Part 6), so a start-up bank with accumulated losses cannot pay any. Check both tests before approving a distribution.

checklist: **Obtain the bank's current Pillar 2A / s.97F capital notice**, its liquidity category designation and the board-approved internal trigger levels, and hold them in a controlled register.

**Build a capital-runway calendar** with Finance: monthly CET1 projections against the board trigger, plus the lead time for a parent injection (board and shareholder resolutions, allotment and any HKMA engagement).
**Review parent support documents** (letter of comfort, capital support agreement) and confirm that planned injections will qualify as CET1.
**Screen every intra-group arrangement** (service fees, guarantees, deposits with or loans to group companies) against the connected-exposure rules and arm's-length terms before signing.
**Embed legal review in regulatory reporting governance**: attestations, treatment of manual adjustments, and a protocol for notifying the HKMA of errors and restating returns.
**Test every proposed distribution** (dividends, discretionary bonuses, AT1 coupons) against the buffer stack (Cap. 155L ss.3F–3K) and the Companies Ordinance (Cap. 622) distributable-profits rule.
**Brief the board each year** on the ICAAP, stress-test results and capital and liquidity triggers, and make sure the minutes record real challenge.
**Track HKMA consultations and amendments** to Cap. 155L, 155Q and 155S, and map each change to a system change request and owner.
itAngle: **Rules engine:** The capital and RWA engine is effectively a rules engine that encodes Cap. 155L. Treat each rule amendment like a release: trace each provision to calculation logic, then to a test case, then to the cell in the return. Counsel can own the interpretation log for that release.

**Returns as statements:** Regulatory returns are legal statements to the regulator. Insist on documented data lineage from the core ledger to each return, automated reconciliations and four-eyes control over manual overrides, in line with BCBS 239 data-aggregation principles.
**Entity resolution:** Large-exposure and connected-exposure monitoring is an entity-resolution problem. Grouping counterparties correctly needs reliable data on corporate hierarchies and control.

**Run velocity:** Deposits can leave at app speed over FPS, 24x7. Liquidity monitoring and stress scenarios should model weekend and intraday outflows at digital run velocity, not branch-era assumptions.
**Capitalised software:** Capitalised software is generally deducted from CET1 as an intangible asset, so build, buy or SaaS decisions have regulatory capital consequences as well as accounting ones.
virtualBankNotes: **No lighter regime:** A digital bank is a licensed bank and is subject to the same capital, liquidity and exposure rules. There is no lighter prudential regime, and the HK$300 million minimum paid-up capital for licensed banks applies.

**Start-up losses:** Start-up losses erode CET1 every month. The HKMA expects shareholders to stand behind the bank, and its digital bank guidance cautions against aggressive growth funded by sustained losses.
**Liquidity category:** Digital banks are typically category 2 institutions for liquidity (LMR-based) unless the MA designates otherwise. Confirm the bank's actual designation.
**Surplus funds:** A deposit-rich, loan-light balance sheet pushes surplus funds into interbank placements and securities. Concentration there can reach large-exposure limits.
pitfalls: **Equity versus capital:** Treating accounting equity as regulatory capital, and overlooking CET1 deductions for deferred tax assets on tax losses and for capitalised software and other intangibles.
**Headline minimums:** Assuming the headline Basel minimums plus buffers are the binding floor, when the confidential Pillar 2A add-on and board triggers sit higher.
**Informal parent support:** Relying on informal parent support (comfort letters, emails) as if it were capital that will arrive on time in a crisis.
**Quiet fixes:** Letting finance teams fix return errors quietly instead of following a defined notification and restatement process with the HKMA.

glossary.definition: Common Equity Tier 1: ordinary shares, share premium, retained earnings and disclosed reserves, less regulatory deductions such as intangibles and certain deferred tax assets. It is the highest-quality capital and absorbs losses first.
Risk-weighted assets: the bank's exposures weighted for credit, market, operational and CVA risk under the Capital Rules. RWA is the denominator of the capital ratios.
The supervisory review layer, in which the HKMA assesses risks not fully captured by the Pillar 1 formulae and sets bank-specific add-ons (a binding Pillar 2A minimum and a Pillar 2B buffer).
A 2.5% of RWA layer of CET1 held above the minimum. If the bank's capital falls into it, automatic restrictions on distributions apply.

A time-varying CET1 buffer that authorities set for each jurisdiction according to credit conditions. A bank's applicable rate is the weighted average of the rates where its private-sector credit exposures sit.
A Basel III limit on the benefit of internal models: total RWA cannot fall below a set percentage (72.5% when fully phased in) of RWA calculated under the standardised approaches.

Liquidity Maintenance Ratio: Hong Kong's local liquidity metric for category 2 institutions, comparing liquefiable assets with qualifying short-term liabilities. The minimum is 25%, measured as a monthly average.
Tier 1 capital divided by an unweighted measure of on- and off-balance-sheet exposures. The minimum is 3%, as a backstop to risk-based ratios.

title: Technology & outsourcing
oneLiner: For a digital bank, technology and vendor failures are banking failures; HKMA expects them governed, contracted and reported.
keyPoints: For a bank with no branches, technology is the bank: accounts, payments and every customer interaction run on code, cloud services and third-party vendors.
**Where the rules sit:** The Banking Ordinance says little about IT directly. The rules that actually apply sit in the HKMA's [[Supervisory Policy Manual]] and circulars.
**What applies:** TM-G-1 (technology risk), TM-E-1 (e-banking), SA-2 (outsourcing), OR-1, OR-2 and TM-G-2 (operational risk, resilience and continuity), and the [[C-RAF]] cyber assessment.

**Statutory overlay:** Since 1 January 2026, Cap. 653 has added statutory cyber duties for designated [[critical infrastructure operators|critical infrastructure operator]], and PDPO DPP4 governs personal data security throughout.
**Why the rules exist:** Operational failure at a bank harms depositors and payment systems quickly.
**Counsel's job:** Turn the rules into contracts, governance records, incident playbooks and accurate, timely notifications to the regulator.

deepDive.heading: Status of the rules
deepDive.lede: The SPM mixes [[statutory guidelines|statutory guideline]] issued under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance with non-statutory guidance notes.
points: **Statutory guideline:** TM-E-1 (V.4, October 2024).
**Guidance notes:** SA-2 (2001), TM-G-1 (2003) and OR-2 (2022).

**Practical difference:** In practice the difference is small: the HKMA tests whether the bank continues to meet the Seventh Schedule minimum criteria, including adequate systems of control, against all of them.
**Consequences:** Persistent shortfalls feed into CAMEL ratings and, ultimately, s.52 directions.
deepDive.takeaway: Treat every 'should' as an expectation: meet it, or depart from it on a documented basis the board can see.

deepDive.heading: Outsourcing and cloud
deepDive.lede: Outsourcing is where counsel earns their keep.

points: **Advance discussion:** SA-2 (2001) expects the bank to discuss with the HKMA in advance any plan to begin outsourcing a banking-related business area (back office included) or to change its scope, and to satisfy the HKMA that the section 2 issues are addressed (para 1.3.2). The digital bank guideline asks for advance discussion of [[material outsourcing]] (para 23).

**Agreements should:** give the HKMA and auditors access and inspection rights, protect customer data, and support contingency and exit (SA-2); TM-G-1 7.1.1 adds that the bank should consider requiring notice of, or approval for, significant sub-contracting.
**Offshore processing:** must not impede HKMA access to data.
**Cloud:** Read SA-2 with the Practice Guide on Cloud Adoption (8 January 2026), reported to replace the 2022 cloud guidance.
deepDive.takeaway: Hyperscalers' standard terms rarely deliver all of this without a financial-services addendum.

deepDive.heading: Operational resilience under OR-2
deepDive.lede: OR-2 (May 2022) implements the Basel operational resilience principles.

visual.caption: Examiners ask for board approvals and test evidence, not policies.

items.label: Tolerance for disruption
items.note: At least a time-based metric

items.label: Its dependencies
items.note: People, processes, technology, information, facilities; third-party and intragroup

points: **Critical operations:** The bank should identify its [[critical operations|critical operation]] and set a [[tolerance for disruption]] for each, with at least a time-based metric (OR-2 4.1.1, 4.2.1).

**Mapping and testing:** It should map the people, processes, technology, information and facilities behind each, including third-party and intragroup dependencies, and test regularly against severe but plausible scenarios (OR-2 5.1, 7.1).
**Deadline:** The 31 May 2026 deadline (OR-2 9.2.3) has passed; the HKMA's June 2026 letter reports that all AIs met it.
**Business as usual:** The letter expects resilience to be sustained as business as usual.
deepDive.takeaway: Examiners ask for board approvals and test evidence, not policies.

deepDive.heading: Incident reporting tracks
deepDive.lede: Incident reporting runs on parallel tracks.
points: **HKMA:** expects immediate notice of significant incidents with whatever facts are available; waiting for root cause can itself draw a finding.

**Cap. 653:** If the bank has been designated, statutory deadlines for notifying the Commissioner also apply: 12 hours if the incident has disrupted, is disrupting or is likely to disrupt the core function of the critical infrastructure, 48 hours in any other case, then a written report within 14 days (s.28; Sch. 6).
**Other tracks:** PDPO, police and customer communications each follow their own rules.
deepDive.takeaway: Build one triage tree that starts every clock at once.

deepDive.heading: E-banking authentication and AI
points: **Bound devices:** The HKMA's 2025 'E-Banking Security ABC' measures make in-app [[bound device]] authentication the default for mobile app users instead of SMS OTP. They build on TM-E-1, which requires two-factor authentication for high-risk transactions and extra controls where one device both runs the app and receives one-time passwords.
**GenAI:** The August 2024 GenAI circular applies governance, fairness, transparency and privacy principles to customer-facing AI.

provisions.title: General Principles for Technology Risk Management
provisions.summary: Non-statutory guidance note (V.1, 24 June 2003) setting baseline expectations for technology risk governance, information security, system development and change management, IT operations and management of technology service providers.
provisions.counselNote: This is the baseline the HKMA uses to judge whether IT controls are 'adequate'. It is old, so the HKMA reads it alongside later modules and circulars, and you should too when advising on control gaps.

provisions.title: Outsourcing
provisions.summary: Sets HKMA expectations for outsourcing (dated 28 December 2001): board accountability, risk assessment and due diligence, written agreements, confidentiality of customer data, monitoring and control, contingency planning, HKMA access, and additional issues for overseas outsourcing. AIs intending to begin outsourcing a banking-related business area (back office included), or to change the scope of such outsourcing, should discuss their plans with the HKMA in advance and satisfy it that the section 2 issues are addressed before implementing (para 1.3.2). It is a non-statutory guidance note (V.1).
provisions.counselNote: This is the main source of the HKMA's expected clauses in vendor contracts, in particular supervisory inspection and access rights. The digital bank guideline adds its own outsourcing paragraph (para 23), asking for advance discussion of material outsourcing and a demonstration that SA-2 will be complied with. Build the HKMA discussion into procurement timelines. See the Vendors tab for the clause-by-clause view.

provisions.title: Operational Resilience
provisions.summary: Non-statutory guidance note issued on 31 May 2022, together with a revised TM-G-2 on business continuity planning, to implement the Basel Committee's March 2021 Principles for Operational Resilience; a revised OR-1 on operational risk management followed on 25 July 2022. AIs were to develop their operational resilience framework by 31 May 2023 and be operationally resilient by 31 May 2026.
provisions.counselNote: The deadline has passed. The HKMA's letter 'Operational Resilience: Sustaining and Uplifting' (June 2026) reports that, on its survey, all AIs met it, and shifts the focus to sustaining and improving resilience. Expect examiners to test board ownership of critical operations, tolerances, dependency mapping (including vendors) and scenario testing. The dates follow from the final module (V.1, 31 May 2022): one year from issue to develop the framework, then up to three more years to become operationally resilient (OR-2 9.2.1, 9.2.3). OR-2 names TM-G-2 and OR-1 as related guidance (OR-2 6.3) but not their revision dates; check those against the HKMA's issuing circulars (not supplied).

provisions.title: Risk Management of E-banking
provisions.summary: Revised version (V.4, 25 October 2024), a statutory guideline under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance. It superseded V.3 (2019), V.2 (2015) and the 26 May 2016 circular on internet banking security controls. It includes guidance on controls over payment card transactions (subsection 7.6).
provisions.counselNote: This is the core rulebook for a digital-only bank's customer channels, covering authentication, fraud monitoring and mobile app security. The HKMA's April 2025 'E-Banking Security ABC' measures build on it: 'Authenticate in-App' makes bound-device authentication the default for mobile app users instead of SMS OTP (due by Q4 2025), and an August 2025 letter extended the package to 'ABCD' by adding deepfake detection.

provisions.title: Security of personal data, including at data processors
provisions.summary: DPP4(1) requires all practicable steps to protect personal data against unauthorized or accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use, having regard to the kind of data, where it is stored, security built into equipment, the integrity and competence of people with access, and secure transmission. DPP4(2) adds that a data user who engages a data processor, in or outside Hong Kong, must adopt contractual or other means to prevent the same risks to data transferred to the processor.
provisions.counselNote: DPP4(2) is why every vendor that touches customers' personal data needs security terms in its contract. It applies to cloud and SaaS providers, outsourced call centres and offshore processors alike.

provisions.title: Data processors: no longer than necessary
provisions.summary: DPP2(2) requires all practicable steps so that personal data is not kept longer than necessary for its purpose. DPP2(3) adds that a data user who engages a data processor, in or outside Hong Kong, must adopt contractual or other means to prevent data transferred to the processor being kept longer than necessary for processing it. DPP2(4) defines a data processor as a person who processes personal data on behalf of another and not for its own purposes.
provisions.counselNote: Together with DPP4(2), this makes retention and return-or-erase terms a legal requirement in vendor contracts, not just good practice. A vendor that uses the data for its own purposes is not a data processor, and the analysis changes.

provisions.title: Liability for employees and agents
provisions.summary: Acts done by an employee in the course of employment, or by an agent with the principal's authority, are treated for the purposes of the Ordinance as done by the employer or principal as well. An employer has a defence if it took practicable steps to prevent the employee's act. The section does not apply to criminal proceedings.
provisions.counselNote: Where a vendor acts as the bank's agent (collection agents, referral or marketing partners), its PDPO breaches can be attributed to the bank. Contract controls and monitoring are the bank's practical protection.

provisions.instrument: Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance (Cap. 653)
provisions.title: Critical infrastructure cybersecurity duties
provisions.summary: In force from 1 January 2026. Operators designated as critical infrastructure operators, including in the banking and financial services sector, bear three categories of duties for their designated critical computer systems: organisational, preventive (such as annual risk assessments and two-yearly audits), and incident reporting and response. Incidents that have disrupted, are disrupting or are likely to disrupt the core function must be notified to the Commissioner of Critical Infrastructure (Computer-system Security) within 12 hours of becoming aware, others within 48 hours, followed by a written report within 14 days (s.28; Sch. 6). The HKMA is the designated authority for the banking and financial services sector and administers the organisational and preventive obligations of operators in that sector.
provisions.counselNote: Designation is by written notice, so confirm whether the bank or any of its systems has been designated. If it has, statutory deadlines and audit and risk-assessment cycles apply on top of HKMA expectations; read the HKMA's Code of Practice for designated AIs (2 June 2026) with the Ordinance. An HKMA–Commissioner MoU dated 29 May 2026 coordinates the two regulators.

provisions.instrument: HKMA circular: Incident response and management procedures
provisions.title: Reporting significant incidents to the HKMA
provisions.summary: Reminds AIs to maintain an effective capability to respond to significant incidents and to notify the HKMA immediately on becoming aware of one, without waiting until the problem has been fixed. AIs should also notify affected customers and consider a public announcement where the situation warrants. Later HKMA letters, such as the 12 August 2014 circular on disruptions of critical banking services, point back to it.
provisions.counselNote: The HKMA has not published a list of notifiable incidents, so the bank must judge significance itself. Write internal significance criteria, have management endorse them and apply them consistently, because those criteria are what examiners will test.

provisions.instrument: HKMA Practice Guide on Cloud Adoption
provisions.title: Cloud adoption expectations
provisions.summary: Combines high-level principles drawn from relevant SPM modules with good practices the HKMA has observed in supervision, following a lifecycle approach. It expands the cloud-related domains covered from four to eight and is reported to supersede the HKMA's 2022 cloud computing guidance.
provisions.counselNote: Read it with SA-2 on every cloud deal. The HKMA notes that cloud projects make up about 80% of reportable technology outsourcing initiatives, so expect scrutiny of concentration risk, security, resilience and exit.

provisions.title: C-RAF and CFI 2.0
provisions.summary: CFI 2.0, effective 1 January 2021 and implemented in phases, keeps three pillars: the Cyber Resilience Assessment Framework (inherent risk assessment, maturity assessment and intelligence-led attack simulation testing), a Professional Development Programme, and the Cyber Intelligence Sharing Platform. The 2.0 review streamlined the C-RAF assessment process and refreshed its control principles, which industry summaries say now reflect current incident response and recovery practice.
provisions.counselNote: C-RAF assessments and attack-simulation findings are supervisory deliverables. Agree confidentiality and report-handling terms with testers, and assume the HKMA will read remediation plans.

provisions.instrument: HKMA circular: Consumer Protection in respect of Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
provisions.title: GenAI in customer-facing applications
provisions.summary: Applies the four consumer-protection principles from the HKMA's 5 November 2019 big data analytics and AI circular (governance and accountability, fairness, transparency and disclosure, data privacy and protection) to customer-facing GenAI use, with additional GenAI-specific expectations.
provisions.counselNote: Before any chatbot, robo-advice or AI marketing goes live, check board and senior management accountability, fairness testing, and disclosure to customers. The HKMA–Cyberport GenA.I. Sandbox (launched 13 August 2024, expanded in 2026 as the cross-regulator GenA.I. Sandbox++) provides supervisory feedback but no legal exemption.

checklist: **Build and maintain an outsourcing register** that flags material arrangements, cloud workloads, data locations and sub-contractors, and reconcile it against what has been discussed with the HKMA.

**Adopt a standard financial-services addendum** covering HKMA and auditor access and inspection, data location and retrieval, confidentiality and DPP4 security, sub-contracting consent, prompt incident notification, participation in continuity testing and assisted exit.

**Run vendor due diligence** proportionate to materiality, covering financial standing, security certifications and audit reports, concentration risk and the legal environment of any offshore location.
**Draft one incident triage tree** that starts the HKMA, Cap. 653, PCPD, police and customer-communication workstreams together, with named owners and pre-approved holding statements.

**Confirm whether the bank or any of its systems has been designated** under Cap. 653 and, if so, diarise the statutory obligations and the requirements of the HKMA's Code of Practice for designated AIs.

**Check that board minutes evidence approval** of the critical-operations criteria and list, the tolerances for disruption and the severe but plausible scenarios; that senior management reviewed each testing report; and that significant deficiencies were reported to the board and prioritised for remediation (OR-2 3.2–3.4, 7.4). A board-level committee assigned to operational resilience may act for the board (OR-2 2.2, footnote 2).
**Align customer terms, app flows and disclosures** with bound-device authentication, any permitted SMS OTP fallback and customers' ability to switch off high-risk functions.
**Set up an AI use-case inventory** and a legal sign-off gate that applies the 2019 and 2024 HKMA consumer-protection principles before any customer-facing deployment.
**Run the materiality assessment** (Materiality tab) for every new SaaS or cloud deployment and every change of scope, and file the note in the outsourcing register before procurement signs.

**Keep an incident call sheet** (Incidents tab) with a named owner for each track: vendor escalation, the HKMA, the Commissioner if the bank is designated, the SFC and HKMA if it is registered, the PCPD, customers and the police.
itAngle: **Cloud audit rights:** SA-2 access rights become engineering requirements: log retention periods, exportable data formats, documented data-retrieval runbooks, and evidence packs (e.g. SOC 2 or ISO 27001 reports, pooled audits) to make audit rights workable in a multi-tenant cloud.

**Dependency mapping:** OR-2 mapping is dependency graphing at the business-service level. Think end-to-end service maps (CMDB plus third-party and people dependencies), with tolerances that resemble RTO/RPO but are measured from the customer's point of view.
**Severity mapping:** Cap. 653 reporting clocks start on 'awareness', so SOC/SIEM severity levels should map to legal severity classes, and the triage decision should be time-stamped and logged.

**Authentication model:** Bound-device authentication relies on keys held in the phone's secure hardware plus app integrity checks; SMS OTP is exposed to SIM swap and malware interception. Liability terms for unauthorised transactions should match the authentication model actually deployed.

**Open API:** The Open API Framework (July 2018; four phases running from product information to transactions) makes onboarding third-party developers a due-diligence and consent-management exercise as well as an API-security one.
virtualBankNotes: **Material outsourcing:** Cloud-native core banking and heavy reliance on vendors mean most core services are likely to be material outsourcing. HKMA pre-consultation is therefore a standing workstream, not an occasional event, so build it into product and procurement timelines.

**App outages:** With no branches, an app or cloud outage takes down every customer channel at once. Continuity plans need alternative ways to reach customers and a manual fallback for urgent requests.
**Group services:** Shared services from a parent technology group are still outsourcing. They need SA-2 terms, HKMA access rights and exit planning like any external vendor.
**Sandboxes:** Digital banks are natural candidates for the Fintech Supervisory Sandbox and the GenA.I. Sandbox. Participation brings supervisory feedback but no exemption from legal requirements.
pitfalls: **Standard cloud terms:** Signing a cloud or SaaS provider's standard terms without HKMA access, sub-contracting and exit provisions, then trying to add them at renewal.
**Late notification:** Waiting for root-cause analysis before notifying the HKMA, or notifying only one authority when several clocks are running.
**Disaster-recovery framing:** Treating OR-2 as an IT disaster-recovery exercise owned by the CIO, instead of business-service tolerances owned by the board.
**Privilege loss:** Letting IT commission forensic and penetration-test reports directly, which weakens any privilege claim and creates drafts the HKMA may later ask to see.

glossary.definition: The HKMA's collection of supervisory guidance, organised in coded modules such as TM-G-1, SA-2 and OR-2. Each module is either a statutory guideline or a non-statutory guidance note.

A guideline issued by the Monetary Authority under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance. It is not law in itself, but non-compliance is relevant to whether an institution continues to meet the authorization criteria.

Outsourcing whose failure or disruption could materially affect the bank's business, customers or compliance. The digital bank guideline asks for advance discussion of material outsourcing with the HKMA (para 23); SA-2 itself asks for advance discussion of outsourcing any banking-related business area, without a materiality test (para 1.3.2).

Under OR-2, activities, processes and services, and the people, technology, information and facilities that support them, whose disruption could pose material risks to the bank's viability or affect its role in the Hong Kong financial system.

The maximum level of disruption to a critical operation the bank can accept, beyond which its viability or its role in the Hong Kong financial system is at risk. It includes at least a time-based metric. Senior management develops it; the board approves it and reviews it at least annually or on major operational change (OR-2 1.3, 3.3, 4.2.1).

Cyber Resilience Assessment Framework: the HKMA's risk-based framework for assessing banks' cyber resilience, made up of an inherent risk assessment, a maturity assessment and intelligence-led cyber attack simulation testing (iCAST).

Under Cap. 653, an operator designated by written notice as responsible for a critical infrastructure in a specified sector. Designation brings organisational, preventive, and incident reporting and response duties.
A customer's mobile device registered to their banking app through a secure binding process. It is used to authenticate logins and high-risk transactions instead of SMS one-time passwords.

intro: **Why it matters:** a digital bank delivers its services exclusively or primarily through electronic channels (Digital Bank Guideline para 1), so many of its critical services are likely to depend on vendors' people, code or cloud (an observation, not a statement in the sources). An outsourcing must not compromise the Seventh Schedule minimum criteria, which require adequate systems of control and business carried on with integrity, prudence and competence and not to the detriment of depositors (SA-2 1.2.2).

**Accountability stays with the bank:** the board and management keep ultimate accountability for anything outsourced; only day-to-day management moves to the vendor (SA-2 2.1.1). The Code of Banking Practice adds that banks should be responsible and accountable for their authorized agents and third-party service providers (2.5).

**Kinds of rule:** statutes bind directly. The PDPO requires the bank to use contractual or other means to control retention and security whenever it engages a data processor (DPP2(3), DPP4(2)), and the AMLO keeps CDD and record-keeping duties with the bank even when a vendor, agent or intermediary does the work (Sch. 2 ss.18, 20–21). The AML/CFT Guideline is a statutory guideline in which every 'must' and 'should' is mandatory (para 1.6). SA-2, TM-G-1 and OR-2 are non-statutory guidance notes; falling short can bear on whether the bank still meets the Seventh Schedule criteria. The Code of Banking Practice is a non-statutory industry code whose compliance the HKMA expects and monitors. The pill on each clause shows its main source (the one listed first); each card lists every source and its legal force.

**Digital banks specifically:** the MA does not object in principle to outsourcing, including to group companies. Digital banks should discuss material outsourcing with the MA in advance and demonstrate that SA-2 will be complied with. The MA must be satisfied on security controls, the confidentiality and integrity of customer information, the PDPO and common-law confidentiality, and that its powers (in particular s.52) will not be hindered; and it should have the right to inspect the provider's security arrangements and controls, or obtain reports from its supervisor, external auditors or other experts (para 23).

**Scope is wide:** SA-2 covers services the bank used to do itself and new ones, providers in Hong Kong or overseas, and group entities as well as third parties (SA-2 1.1.1). OR-2 asks for dependencies on third parties and intragroup entities to be managed as they would be under outsourcing arrangements (OR-2 6.2).

lifecycle.caption: SA-2 sections 1.3 and 2; in on-site examinations, off-site reviews and prudential interviews, the HKMA checks whether the section 2 concerns have been addressed and deficiencies rectified (SA-2 1.3.6).

items.label: Assess
items.note: Criticality of the service, reasons for outsourcing, effect on operational, legal and reputation risk

items.label: Due diligence
items.note: Financial soundness, reputation, technical and operational capability, banking experience

items.label: Discuss with the HKMA
items.note: In advance, before outsourcing a banking-related area or changing its scope

items.label: Contract
items.note: PDPO and AMLO duties are legal requirements; AML Guideline terms are mandatory; SA-2 and Code terms are expected

items.label: Monitor
items.note: Performance, material problems, financial condition and contingency plan; risk assessment and agreement reviewed regularly

items.label: Exit
items.note: Data retrieved or destroyed; alternative providers or an in-house fallback considered and costed

terms.title: Scope and service levels
terms.summary: The agreement should clearly set out the type and level of services and the vendor's contractual obligations (SA-2 2.4.1). The liabilities that 2.4.1 also mentions are dealt with under Liability, indemnities and insurance. Concrete, measurable service levels are what let the bank monitor performance against target (2.3.2).
require: **Services:** the type and level of services to be provided, clearly set out (SA-2 2.4.1). Describing them precisely enough to monitor is counsel's drafting point.

**Service levels:** SA-2 expects controls to monitor the vendor's performance continuously, giving comparison with a target service level as an example (2.3.2), and the level of services set out in the agreement (2.4.1). Measurable targets in the contract are the practical way to meet both (inference).
**Obligations:** the vendor's contractual obligations, clearly set out (SA-2 2.4.1). Its liability for failing to meet them is covered under Liability, indemnities and insurance.
**Technology services:** the provider's performance standards, and who owns the software and hardware used (TM-G-1 7.1.1).
**Software packages:** ongoing maintenance and adequate support, specified in a formal contract (TM-G-1 4.2.6).

sources.label: SPM OR-2 Operational resilience
sources.note: Non-statutory guidance note; V.1, 31 May 2022 (the final module you supplied).

drafting: **Critical operations:** set recovery-time and availability commitments that fit inside the tolerance for disruption the board has approved for the operation the service supports (counsel's inference from OR-2 3.3 and 4.2.1; the module does not say this of contracts).
**Service credits:** treat them as a pricing adjustment, not a remedy; keep termination and step-in rights for persistent failure.
**Remedies:** state that service credits are without prejudice to the bank's other rights; caps, exclusions, indemnities and insurance are dealt with under Liability, indemnities and insurance.
terms.cloud: Standard cloud terms often commit only to availability, backed by service credits (market practice, not from the sources). Negotiate support-response and incident-notification commitments separately.

playbook.why: The core is SA-2 2.4.1: the type and level of services should be clearly set out in the agreement, with TM-G-1 7.1.1 and 4.2.6 adding performance standards, ownership and software support. Both are non-statutory guidance notes, so a gap needs a documented rationale and sign-off rather than being a legal breach.
preferred: **Defined Services:** a services schedule describing the Services, deliverables, dependencies and the Bank's own responsibilities precisely enough to monitor and audit against (SA-2 2.4.1, 2.3.2).

**Measurable service levels:** availability, response, resolution and support levels for the Bank's Services, with a stated measurement method and reporting under the reporting clause. For Critical Services, availability here and recovery objectives under the continuity clause, both within the operation's tolerance for disruption (inference from OR-2 3.3, 4.2.1).

**Ownership and support:** the contract states who owns the software and hardware used for the Services, and commits the Supplier to ongoing maintenance and adequate support of the software packages and versions the Bank uses (TM-G-1 7.1.1, 4.2.6).

**Persistent failure:** service credits are a price adjustment that leaves other remedies intact and counts towards damages for the same failure. Repeated misses across any service levels, or a severe miss of a key one, give a termination right without a cure period (counsel's drafting).
fallback: **Supplier's standard SLA:** acceptable for non-critical Services if it is measurable, reported at least monthly, attached in the version signed, and cannot be reduced during the term without the Bank's consent (see the change-control clause).
**Credits for minor misses:** service credits as the only financial remedy for minor misses is acceptable only if serious or repeated failure still gives damages and a termination right.
**Licence, not ownership:** where the Supplier keeps its platform, a licence is acceptable if the Bank owns Bank Data and Bank-specific deliverables and the licence runs through any Exit Period.

**Support by policy:** support terms in the Supplier's support policy are acceptable if the version at signing is attached and later changes cannot reduce support for software versions the Bank uses or shorten the notice before support ends.
redLines: **Undefined service:** do not sign where the Services or service levels are left to Supplier documents it can change at will; SA-2 expects the type and level of services to be clearly set out in the agreement (SA-2 2.4.1).

**Critical Services without commitments:** do not sign for a Critical Service without contractual availability commitments here and recovery objectives under the continuity clause, both checked against the Bank's tolerance for disruption (OR-2 4.2.1, 6.2; counsel's drafting).
**Unsupported core software:** do not rely on mission-critical software packages with no contractual maintenance and support commitment (TM-G-1 4.2.6).
model: (a) The Supplier shall provide the Services described in [Schedule 1] in accordance with this Agreement, Applicable Law [so far as it applies to the Supplier or the Services] and the Bank policies and regulatory requirements listed in [Schedule 2], and shall maintain sufficient resources and expertise to do so throughout the term. New regulatory requirements are added under [the change-control clause].

(b) The Supplier shall meet or exceed the service levels in [Schedule 3], measure its performance against them for the Bank's Services specifically, by the methods set out there, and report on them under [the reporting clause].

(c) For each Critical Service, the Supplier shall meet the availability commitments in [Schedule 3, Part B] and the recovery objectives under [the continuity clause]. The Supplier shall agree, under [the change-control clause], any reasonable change the Bank requires to keep those commitments within the tolerance for disruption the Bank has set for the operation concerned.

(d) For each missed service level, the Supplier shall give the service credits in [Schedule 3], investigate the root cause and implement a remediation plan the Bank approves. Service credits are a price adjustment, do not limit any other right or remedy of the Bank, and shall be taken into account in assessing damages for the same failure.

(e) If the Supplier misses service levels [three] times in any [six]-month period, whether or not the same service level, or misses a key service level identified in [Schedule 3] [by more than the margin stated there], the Bank may terminate the affected Services by notice, without a cure period and without termination charge or other liability.

(f) [Schedule 4] sets out, as between the parties, who owns each item of software and hardware used for the Services. The Supplier shall maintain and support all software packages used for the Services, at the levels in [Schedule 3], while the Bank uses them, covering at least the current and previous major versions, and shall give [24] months' notice before support for any version the Bank uses ends.
watchFor: **Moving documents:** service descriptions, SLAs or support policies incorporated by a web link the Supplier can update unilaterally, or end-of-support dates set on short notice, so the agreed level can fall without the Bank's consent.

**Sole remedy:** wording making service credits the Bank's 'sole and exclusive remedy' for any service failure, cutting off damages and termination for persistent or serious failure, or credits forfeited unless claimed within a short window and capped at a small share of fees.

**Measurement gaps:** availability averaged across the whole platform, with broad exclusions such as maintenance at the Supplier's discretion, so that an outage affecting the Bank never registers as a miss.
**Targets, not commitments:** service levels described as 'targets' or 'objectives', or support limited to 'commercially reasonable efforts' with no response or resolution times.

pushback.says: Our SLA is standard for all customers and can't be changed.
pushback.reply: We can start from your standard. But the HKMA expects the level of service to be clearly set out in our agreement (SA-2 2.4.1), so fix the version we sign, stop unilateral reductions, and add availability and recovery commitments for the Critical Services.

pushback.says: Service credits are your remedy for downtime; we won't accept termination for SLA misses.
pushback.reply: Credits are fine for minor misses, and we will set them against any damages for the same failure, so there is no double recovery. For persistent failure we need a way out: we should not continue an arrangement that may weaken the resilience of our critical operations (OR-2 6.2). The threshold need not be a hair trigger.

pushback.says: Ownership of our platform is not negotiable.
pushback.reply: We are not asking to own it. TM-G-1 expects the agreement to deal clearly with software and hardware ownership (7.1.1); the schedule just needs to say what is yours, what is ours, and what licence we keep through exit.

playbook.escalate: Suggested: deviations affecting Critical Services to the Head of Legal with the CRO or the outsourcing committee; other deviations to the business owner with Legal and Procurement, recorded in the outsourcing risk assessment.

terms.title: Liability, indemnities and insurance
terms.summary: SA-2 asks for the provider's contractual liabilities, not only its obligations, to be clearly set out in the service agreement (2.4.1). Liability terms move cost, not accountability, which stays with the bank (2.1.1). Caps, carve-outs, indemnities and insurance should leave the bank able to recover what a vendor failure is likely to cost it.
require: **Liabilities set out:** the vendor's contractual liabilities, as well as its obligations, clearly set out in the service agreement (SA-2 2.4.1). SA-2 says nothing on the size of caps; that is a commercial judgment.

**Confidentiality remedy:** among the typical safeguards for customer data, SA-2 lists the bank's contractual rights to take action against the vendor for a breach of confidentiality (2.5.2). A cap or exclusion that leaves such a breach effectively without remedy undercuts that safeguard (inference).

**Accountability stays:** the board and management keep ultimate accountability for the outsourced activity (SA-2 2.1.1), and banks should be responsible and accountable for their third-party service providers (CoBP 2.5). Indemnities and caps share cost between the parties; they do not move that accountability.

**Customer losses:** unless a customer acts fraudulently or with gross negligence, the MA's view is that the customer should not bear direct loss from unauthorized transactions (Digital Bank Guideline para 22). Where a vendor failure causes such loss, the bank pays first, so it needs recovery from the vendor (inference).

**Data protection claims:** an individual who suffers damage, including injury to feelings, from a data user's contravention of the PDPO is entitled to compensation from that data user, subject to a reasonable-care defence (PDPO s.66). Where the vendor acts as the bank's agent with its authority, its acts are treated as the bank's too (s.65(2)). The bank may face such claims for a vendor's failure (inference).

**Statutory control of caps:** liability for death or personal injury from negligence cannot be excluded. Other negligence liability, and liability for breach where the bank contracts on the vendor's written standard terms, can be excluded or restricted only so far as reasonable; the vendor must prove that, and for a fixed-sum cap its resources and insurability count (Cap. 71 ss.3(5)-(6), 7, 8). Sections 7 to 9 do not apply so far as the contract relates to creating or transferring IP rights (Sch. 1 para 1(c)), and ss.7 to 12 do not operate where Hong Kong law governs only by the parties' choice (s.17).

**Insurance and ability to pay:** due diligence covers the vendor's financial soundness (SA-2 2.3.1), and monitoring includes regular review of its financial condition (2.6.2); a cap is only as good as the vendor's ability to pay. TM-G-1 refers banks to TM-G-2 (not supplied) on adequate insurance coverage of IT resources (5.4.1) but does not mention vendors' insurance, so requiring vendor cover, or a parent guarantee for a thin entity, is counsel's drafting.

**Fines:** an indemnity for fines or penalties imposed on the bank because of the vendor's breach, such as a pecuniary penalty under AMLO s.21, is good practice only so far as the law allows; public policy may bar recovering a penalty for the bank's own culpable conduct (general law, not checked here).

sources.label: SPM TM-G-1 Technology risk
sources.note: Refers banks to TM-G-2 (not supplied) on detailed recovery procedures and on ensuring adequate insurance coverage of IT resources. It does not address vendors' insurance.

sources.label: Digital Bank Guideline
sources.note: Issued under s.16(10) of the Banking Ordinance, not s.7(3). The MA's view on who bears direct loss from unauthorized transactions.

sources.label: Code of Banking Practice (Dec 2023)
sources.note: Institutions should be responsible and accountable for the actions of their authorized agents and third-party service providers.

sources.label: PDPO (Cap. 486)
sources.note: s.66: compensation from the data user for damage, including injury to feelings, caused by its contravention, subject to the defence of having taken reasonable care (s.66(3)). s.65(2): acts of an agent acting with the principal's authority are treated as the principal's as well (not for criminal proceedings, s.65(4)).

sources.label: Control of Exemption Clauses Ordinance (Cap. 71)
sources.note: Applies to business liability (s.2(2)). s.3(5): for a cap at a specified sum, the court considers the resources available to meet the liability and how far insurance was open. Sch. 1 para 1(c) takes contracts out of ss.7 to 9 so far as they relate to creating or transferring IP rights.

sources.label: AMLO (Cap. 615)
sources.note: The relevant authority may order a financial institution to pay a pecuniary penalty for contravening a specified provision. An example of a penalty imposed on the bank itself.

drafting: **Size from the scenario:** set caps from a costed breach scenario (customer compensation, Incident response, notifications, replacement services), not from the annual fee; a low-fee service can still hold high-impact data.

**Carve-outs:** keep fraud, wilful default and abandonment uncapped; put breaches of confidentiality, data protection, security, Incident notification, Cap. 653 and Regulator access or cooperation duties outside the general cap, either uncapped or under a separate, higher cap.

**Direct loss defined:** list as recoverable direct loss the costs of restoring Bank Data, investigating and remediating an Incident, notifying customers and Regulators, compensating customers and obtaining replacement services, so they are not lost as 'indirect' loss.

**Insurance terms:** name the cover types and minimum limits, require reputable insurers, certificates on signing and renewal, notice of cancellation or material reduction, and run-off cover after termination.
terms.cloud: Large cloud providers' standard terms commonly cap liability at fees paid over a recent period and exclude lost data (market practice, not from the sources). Where room to negotiate is limited, prioritise a higher cap or carve-out for confidentiality, data-protection and security breaches, and record any residual risk the bank accepts in its risk assessment (SA-2 2.2.1).

playbook.why: SA-2 2.4.1, a non-statutory guidance note, asks for the provider's contractual liabilities to be clearly set out but sets no level. Caps and insurance are commercial, but a cap that leaves a confidentiality breach without remedy undercuts a safeguard SA-2 2.5.2 lists, and would be hard to justify.
preferred: **Cap with carve-outs:** a general annual cap of at least [200]% of annual charges [or HK$[ ], if greater], with no cap for fraud, wilful default, abandonment, or breach of confidentiality, data-protection, security, Incident notification, Cap. 653 or Regulator cooperation duties, and a lower cap on the Bank's own liability (market practice).

**Losses that matter recoverable:** costs of restoring Bank Data, Incident response, notifying customers and Regulators, customer compensation and replacement services are recoverable direct loss, not excluded as indirect or consequential.

**Indemnities:** the Supplier indemnifies the Bank against third-party claims and regulatory action caused by its or its Subcontractors' breach of confidentiality, data-protection, security or Applicable Law, and against intellectual property claims; fines only so far as the law allows. The Bank keeps conduct of Regulator actions and customer claims.

**Insurance with evidence:** professional indemnity, cyber and data breach, public liability and crime or fidelity cover at stated minimums, with reputable insurers, certificates on signing and renewal, and notice of cancellation (counsel's drafting; compare TM-G-1 5.4.1).
fallback: **Super-cap:** a separate, higher cap for confidentiality, data and security breaches, only if fraud and wilful default stay uncapped and it covers the costed breach scenario. If a major cloud provider will not go that far, record the gap and compensating controls, such as Bank-held keys, and escalate (SA-2 2.2.1).

**Narrower fines indemnity:** dropping the fines indemnity is acceptable if Incident costs, customer compensation and third-party claims caused by the Supplier stay recoverable, since fines may not be recoverable anyway.
**Mutual cap:** a mutual general cap and mutual confidentiality carve-out are acceptable if the Bank's obligation to pay charges sits outside the cap.

**Group insurance or guarantee:** cover under the Supplier group's programme, or a parent's self-insurance, is acceptable if limits available to this contract are evidenced and, for a thinly capitalised Supplier, the parent guarantees performance.
redLines: **Empty remedy:** no cap or exclusion that leaves a breach of confidentiality effectively without remedy; a contractual right to act for breach of confidentiality is a typical SA-2 safeguard (SA-2 2.5.2). Treat data-protection and Regulator cooperation breaches the same way (counsel's drafting).

**Fraud and wilful default:** no limitation or exclusion of liability for fraud or wilful default by the Supplier, a Subcontractor or any of their personnel, or for deliberate abandonment of the Services (counsel's drafting).

**Data loss as indirect loss:** no wording that excludes loss of or damage to Bank Data, or the costs of Incident response and customer remediation, as indirect or consequential loss (counsel's drafting).
model: (a) Subject to paragraphs (b) and (c), the Supplier's total liability for events in any contract year shall not exceed [the greater of HK$[ ] and [200]% of the charges for that year or, in the first year, the forecast charges]. The Bank's liability, other than to pay charges, shall not exceed [100]% of the charges for the year concerned. Service credits count towards neither limit.

(b) Paragraph (a) does not limit liability for: (i) fraud or wilful default by either party, a Subcontractor or their personnel, or abandonment of the Services; (ii) the Supplier's breach of [the confidentiality, data protection, security and Incident clauses]; (iii) its breach of [the Regulator access, audit, cooperation and Cap. 653 clauses]; (iv) the indemnity in paragraph (d); or (v) anything that cannot lawfully be limited. [Liability under (ii) and (iv) shall not exceed HK$[ ] in aggregate.]

(c) Except for liability under paragraph (b)(i), [(ii),] (iv) or (v), neither party is liable for indirect or consequential loss. The following are recoverable direct losses of the Bank: the costs of restoring or recreating Bank Data; investigating and remediating an Incident; notifying customers and any Regulator; compensation reasonably paid to customers; and the reasonable additional cost of replacement services.

(d) The Supplier shall indemnify the Bank against all losses, costs and liabilities from any third-party claim, or any fine, penalty or Regulator action, caused by a breach by the Supplier or a Subcontractor of [the confidentiality, data protection or security clauses] or of Applicable Law, or from any claim that the Services infringe a third party's intellectual property, except so far as the law bars indemnity for a fine or penalty.

(e) The Supplier shall maintain, with reputable insurers, the insurances in [Schedule 7] at no less than the limits stated, during the term and for [3] years after it. It shall provide certificates of insurance on signing, on each renewal and on request, and notify the Bank promptly of any cancellation, reduction or material erosion of cover.

(f) The Supplier's liability is not reduced by any insurance, or by any approval, review or audit by the Bank or a Regulator. The Bank shall have conduct of any Regulator action, and of any claim or complaint by its customers, covered by paragraph (d), and shall consult the Supplier on it. [The Supplier's parent shall guarantee the Supplier's obligations in the form in [Schedule 8].]
watchFor: **One low cap for everything:** a single cap at fees paid in the previous 3 or 12 months applying to all claims, including confidentiality and data breaches, which for a low-fee service can be negligible.

**Data loss excluded:** 'loss of data', 'regulatory fines' or 'remediation costs' listed alongside lost profits as excluded loss, removing the Bank's main heads of recovery after an Incident (see the incident clause).

**Hollow insurance and time bars:** liability limited to 'amounts recovered under our insurance', insurance promises with no stated limits or evidence, or claims barred unless brought within a short period, such as 6 or 12 months after the event.

**Broad contribution defences:** no liability wherever Bank 'instructions', 'configuration' or 'failure to follow recommendations' contributed in any way, instead of liability reduced in proportion to the Bank's share.

pushback.says: Our liability is capped at 12 months' fees for every customer; we can't go higher.
pushback.reply: A fee-based general cap can work, but a confidentiality or data breach costs far more than the fees, and SA-2 lists our right to act for breach of confidentiality as a typical safeguard (2.5.2). Put those breaches outside the general cap, at least under a realistic super-cap. Where the Ordinance applies, a cap in your written standard terms must also be reasonable (Cap. 71 s.8).

pushback.says: Regulatory fines are your responsibility; we don't indemnify them.
pushback.reply: Fines for our own conduct are ours, and the law may not let us recover them. We are asking only for fines and remedial costs caused by your breach, and only so far as the law allows.

pushback.says: Our insurance arrangements are confidential.
pushback.reply: We don't need the policy wording, only certificates showing insurer, cover, limits and period. SA-2 expects us to review your financial condition regularly (2.6.2), and insurance is part of that picture.

playbook.escalate: Suggested: a general cap below [100]% of annual charges, or any cap on confidentiality, data or security breaches below the costed scenario, to the Head of Legal with the CRO; for Critical Services, also to the outsourcing committee.

terms.title: HKMA access and inspection
terms.summary: The HKMA's examination powers under BO ss.55–56 run against the bank (and, for a locally incorporated bank, its branches, offices and subsidiaries), not against a third-party, parent or sister-company vendor. For those vendors, the contract is what gives the HKMA access to the vendor's operations.
require: **Inspection clause:** the agreement allows supervisory inspection or review of the vendor's operations and controls, so far as they relate to the outsourced activity (SA-2 2.8.2).
**Unimpeded access:** access to data by the HKMA's examiners should not be impeded by the outsourcing (SA-2 2.8.2).

**Local banks:** for a locally incorporated bank, a principal HKMA concern is whether it can exercise its Banking Ordinance powers effectively if the service provider gives only limited cooperation (SA-2 2.9.2); this is the basis for a direct-cooperation undertaking.
**Overseas providers:** the HKMA's right of access to data is confirmed in writing by the bank and by its home or host authorities, as the case may be (SA-2 2.9.1).

**Digital bank rule:** the MA should have the right to inspect the security arrangements and other controls at the provider, or to obtain reports from its supervisor, external auditors or other experts (Digital Bank Guideline para 23).

**No hindrance:** the MA must be satisfied that the outsourcing arrangements will not hinder his powers and duties under the Banking Ordinance, in particular s.52, the power of control over an institution: requiring it to take action, or directing that it take advice from an Advisor or be managed by a Manager (para 23).

**Assessment reports:** for critical technology services the bank is expected to commission a detailed assessment of the provider's IT control environment, ideally by a party independent of the provider, and the report should be provided to the HKMA for reference (TM-G-1 7.1.1). E-banking independent assessment reports should be submitted to the HKMA on request (TM-E-1 3.3.1). The confidentiality terms therefore need to permit both disclosures (drafting point).

sources.label: Digital Bank Guideline
sources.note: Issued under s.16(10) of the Banking Ordinance, not s.7(3): it sets the principles the MA applies in authorizing digital banks.

sources.label: Banking Ordinance (Cap. 155)
sources.note: The MA may examine an AI with or without prior notice; the AI must give the examiner access to its books, documents and information.

drafting: **No gatekeeping:** avoid notice periods, cost recovery or scope limits that the vendor could use to delay a supervisory visit; s.55 allows the MA to examine the bank without prior notice.
**Direct cooperation:** have the vendor agree to cooperate with the HKMA directly, not only through the bank.

**Continuity under s.52:** the vendor keeps providing the service, and cooperates, if the MA gives directions or appoints an Advisor or Manager; no termination or suspension merely because those powers are used (counsel's drafting to meet para 23).
terms.cloud: Certifications and pooled audits help the bank's own assurance but do not replace the HKMA's right. Keep that right in the contract expressly.

playbook.why: The Digital Bank Guideline, a statutory guideline under BO s.16(10), says the MA must be satisfied that outsourcing will not hinder his Banking Ordinance powers, in particular s.52, and should be able to inspect the provider's controls or obtain reports on them (para 23). SA-2 2.8.2 adds that the contract should contain an express supervisory-inspection clause.
preferred: **Direct access:** The HKMA, anyone it appoints and any other Regulator the Bank names may inspect the Supplier's and Subcontractors' premises, systems, records, Bank Data and controls for the Services (SA-2 2.8.2; Digital Bank Guideline para 23), at any time, with or without notice, while either holds Bank Data (counsel's drafting, mirroring BO s.55).

**Direct cooperation:** The Supplier deals with the Regulator directly, answering questions and reporting on its controls, and tells the Bank of each contact (counsel's drafting). Digital banks are expected to be locally incorporated (Digital Bank Guideline para 8), and for them SA-2 2.9.2 names a provider's limited cooperation as a principal concern.

**Free disclosure:** The Bank may give the Regulator the contract, information about the Supplier and every audit, assessment or test report on it, including the IT control assessment and the e-banking independent assessment report, whatever terms the report came under (TM-G-1 7.1.1; TM-E-1 3.3.1).

**Powers unhindered:** The Supplier keeps performing, and works with any Advisor or Manager, if the MA uses BO s.52 powers; their use is never a ground to suspend, terminate or reprice (inference from Digital Bank Guideline para 23; see the termination clause). Wilfully obstructing a Manager is an offence (BO s.53H).
fallback: **Notice for routine visits:** Accept [5] Business Days' notice for planned, routine inspections only if the Regulator can still attend at short or no notice whenever it considers it necessary, and scheduling can never be used to delay.

**Reports first:** Accept that the Regulator will normally be offered recent independent reports before any visit, only if the Regulator alone decides whether they are enough. Para 23 lets the MA inspect or obtain reports; that choice must stay with the MA.

**Site rules:** Accept reasonable site-security rules, escorts and protection of other clients' data in shared facilities, only if they never limit what the Regulator can see of the Services, Bank Data or the relevant controls.

**Cost of visits:** Accept reimbursement of the Supplier's reasonable, documented out-of-pocket costs of Regulator visits only if invoiced afterwards, never a condition of access, and not payable where the visit follows an Incident or a Supplier breach (counsel's drafting).
redLines: **Inspection right:** Do not sign without an express right for the HKMA, and anyone it appoints, to inspect or review the Supplier's operations and controls relating to the Services, including its security arrangements, and to obtain reports on them (SA-2 2.8.2; Digital Bank Guideline para 23).

**No hindrance:** No term letting the Supplier refuse or delay access by the HKMA or its appointees to Bank Data wherever held, make it conditional on payment, a contract change or a non-disclosure agreement, or hinder the MA's s.52 powers (Digital Bank Guideline para 23; SA-2 2.8.2). Notice and site rules only on fallback terms.

**Reports to the HKMA:** No confidentiality term, in the contract or in any portal or report-access terms, that stops the Bank submitting to the HKMA, on request, an e-banking independent assessment report covering the Supplier's systems (TM-E-1 3.3.1).
model: (a) Regulator access. The Supplier shall, and shall procure that each Subcontractor shall, give the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), anyone it appoints and any other Regulator the Bank names in writing access at any time, with or without notice, to its premises, personnel, systems, Bank Data, records and information relating to the Services, to inspect, review and copy them, during the term and the Exit Period and while it holds Bank Data.

(b) Cooperation. The Supplier shall cooperate fully and promptly with the Regulator, whether contacted directly or through the Bank, including by answering its questions, making knowledgeable senior staff available and reporting on its security arrangements and other controls for the Services. Unless Applicable Law or the HKMA forbids it, the Supplier shall promptly tell the Bank of each such contact and what it provided, and tell it before any Regulator other than the HKMA accesses Customer Data.

(c) No conditions. The Supplier shall not make access or cooperation under this clause conditional on payment, on any change to this Agreement, or on any confidentiality undertaking by the Regulator beyond its obligations under Applicable Law. [The Bank shall reimburse the Supplier's reasonable, documented out-of-pocket costs of Regulator visits, invoiced afterwards, unless they relate to an Incident or a breach by the Supplier.]

(d) Disclosure to the Regulator. Nothing in this Agreement, or in any terms on which the Supplier makes a report or information available (such as portal terms), restricts the Bank from disclosing to the Regulator this Agreement, any information relating to the Supplier, any Subcontractor or the Services, or any audit, assessment, certification or test report. The Supplier consents to each such disclosure and shall obtain any consent its auditors or assessors require.

(e) Regulatory powers. If a Regulator gives the Bank a direction or requirement, or appoints an Advisor or Manager for the Bank, the Supplier shall continue to perform the Services, act on the instructions of the Bank or, for the affairs under its management, that Manager, and cooperate with that Advisor or Manager. [The termination clause] governs any right to suspend, terminate or change the Services when a Regulator exercises its powers.

(f) Remedies and confirmations. Refusing or materially delaying access or cooperation under this clause is a material breach [that cannot be remedied]. [The HKMA may enforce paragraphs (a) to (c) under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Ordinance (Cap. 623).] The Supplier shall give the Bank any information it needs to obtain or maintain written confirmation of the HKMA's access rights. [The location and governing-law clauses] deal with laws that could prevent compliance.
watchFor: **Bank-only rights:** an audit clause naming only the Bank and its auditors, or admitting the Regulator only 'through the Bank', alongside a blanket exclusion of third-party rights. The HKMA needs its own right; decide deliberately whether it may enforce it under Cap. 623.

**Gatekeeping:** access subject to long notice, business hours only, one visit a year, a scope the Supplier must agree, advance payment, the Regulator signing the Supplier's non-disclosure agreement, or only 'commercially reasonable efforts' to assist.

**Reports in lieu:** wording that the Supplier meets all regulatory access by providing certifications or third-party reports 'in lieu of' inspection. Reports can be the routine route (see fallback), never the only one.

**Hosting-chain gap:** Regulator access promised for the Supplier only, or for Subcontractors only 'to the extent their terms permit', leaving the cloud host that holds Bank Data outside. Require flow-down, or the Supplier's own rights against the host exercised for the Regulator (see the sub-contracting clause).

pushback.says: Our standard audit clause already covers customers. Your regulator can rely on that through you, and our certifications should be enough.
pushback.reply: This is a must-have. The Digital Bank Guideline, a statutory guideline, requires the MA to be satisfied that its powers will not be hindered and expects it to be able to inspect your controls or obtain reports (para 23). BO s.55 reaches us and, as we are locally incorporated, our own branches, offices and subsidiaries, but not a third-party, parent or sister-company supplier like you, so the contract must give the access. Your certifications can be routine evidence, but whether they are enough is the MA's call.

pushback.says: We cannot allow unannounced visits to a shared data centre, and we must charge for time spent on regulators.
pushback.reply: Routine visits will normally be planned, and your site rules and other clients' data will be respected. But notice and payment cannot be conditions: the MA may examine the Bank with or without notice (BO s.55). We can agree to reimburse reasonable, documented out-of-pocket costs, invoiced afterwards.

pushback.says: The HKMA must sign our non-disclosure agreement before it sees anything.
pushback.reply: No. People exercising functions under the Banking Ordinance, including those the MA authorizes, Advisors and Managers, are bound by statutory secrecy, subject to limited exceptions (BO s.120). An extra undertaking would put a condition on access, which is the kind of hindrance para 23 of the Digital Bank Guideline rules out.

playbook.escalate: Suggested: any departure from a red line goes to the Head of Legal and the CRO and then the outsourcing committee; for material outsourcing, consider raising it with the HKMA before signing, since material outsourcing should be discussed with it in advance (Digital Bank Guideline para 23).

terms.title: Audit and assessment rights
terms.summary: The bank's internal and external auditors need unimpeded access to outsourced data (SA-2 2.8.2), and the bank should assess the IT control environment of each provider of critical technology services every year (TM-G-1 7.1.1). The contract has to give them, and the assessors the bank appoints, the access to do this.
require: **Auditors:** access to data by the bank's internal and external auditors should not be impeded by the outsourcing (SA-2 2.8.2). SA-2 asks for an express clause only for supervisory inspection; an equivalent audit-access clause for the bank's auditors is the usual way to deliver this (drafting point).

**Annual assessment:** the bank should conduct an annual assessment confirming the adequacy of the IT control environment of each provider of critical technology services (TM-G-1 7.1.1). The contract should give it the access and information to do this (inference; TM-G-1 does not specify contract terms for this).

**Independent assessment:** cooperation with the rigorous independent assessment that the bank's policies should ensure is performed before a new e-banking delivery channel or major enhancement is launched. Where relevant, it should cover systems or processes outsourced to providers inside or outside the group (TM-E-1 3.3.1).

**Penetration tests:** where the bank's independent-assessment framework does not include penetration tests, regular tests by qualified independent parties assessing, at least annually, the bank's Internet banking and other financial services delivered over the Internet or wireless networks, covering enquiry-only services and relevant outsourced systems (TM-E-1 3.3.2). The tests therefore reach the vendor's relevant systems; the vendor's contractual duty to cooperate with them is the drafting point.

**Vendor-built software:** before launching any Internet banking system or system change, the bank should be satisfied that the vendor has an adequate code review process; otherwise the bank should review the vendor's code itself (TM-E-1 5.3.2, footnote 15). The contract should therefore require evidence of the vendor's review and, failing that, give the bank a right to review the code (drafting point).
drafting: **Remediation:** pair audit rights with an obligation to fix findings within agreed deadlines, and a termination right if they are not fixed.
terms.cloud: Accept certifications and pooled audits as the routine evidence, but keep an on-site or direct audit right for when the evidence is not enough.

playbook.why: Where the Services support the Bank's e-banking, the core is mandatory: TM-E-1, a statutory guideline under BO s.7(3) whose requirements AIs should comply with (1.4.2), says independent assessments and annual penetration tests should cover relevant outsourced systems and vendor-built Internet banking code should be adequately reviewed (3.3.1, 3.3.2, 5.3.2). Otherwise the clause rests on non-statutory guidance (SA-2 2.8.2; TM-G-1 7.1.1) and works at the expected level.
