activities.title: Holding crypto-assets or taking them as collateral on the bank's balance sheet
activities.summary: The bank wants crypto-assets, stablecoin tokens or tokenised assets on its own balance sheet, or wants to accept them as security for a loan. The capital rules sort each exposure into a Basel group, and the group decides the risk weight and whether limits bite.
activities.route: Yes in principle, but only within the Basel-based capital, exposure-limit and disclosure rules in force since 1 January 2026, and in practice after talking to the HKMA first. Crypto that fails the Group 1 and Group 2a conditions defaults to Group 2b, which carries a 1,250% risk weight, so the business case rarely works outside Group 1.
require: **Capital rules:** The MA may make capital rules that give effect to Basel standards, including by adopting Basel documents (Cap. 155 s.97C). The Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025 (L.N. 150 of 2025, gazetted on 11 July 2025) apply the Basel cryptoasset standard from 1 January 2026.

**Classification:** Each exposure is sorted into Group 1a (tokenised traditional assets), Group 1b (assets with effective stabilisation mechanisms) or Group 2. Group 2a covers assets meeting the s.361(4) conditions; the rest are Group 2b. The conditions are in the Banking (Capital) Rules s.361, and the HKMA's module CRP-1 (V.1, effective 1 January 2026) guides their application.

**Group 2b weighting:** Group 2b banking-book exposures take a 1,250% risk weight on the greater of aggregate long and short positions (Capital Rules s.385). Assume near-deduction and no hedge recognition. Group 2a uses modified market-risk approaches instead.

**Group 2 ratio:** Every AI must calculate a group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio (Capital Rules s.387). The 1% limit, with notice, add-on and rectification duties above 1% and 2%, binds only G-SIBs and D-SIBs (s.388). L.N. 152 brings crypto into large-exposure limits.

**Disclosure:** The Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025 (L.N. 151 of 2025) add a cryptoasset disclosure division (Division 8D), including annual qualitative disclosure of crypto activities and classification approach. Failure to comply with disclosure rules is an offence for directors, chief executives and managers (Cap. 155 s.60A).

**Supervisory conditions:** The MA may attach or vary conditions on an authorization, including restrictions on business (Cap. 155 s.16(5), (9)(a)). That is the lever if the HKMA is uneasy about a digital bank's crypto position.
gates: **Classify before you buy:** Obtain a written classification memo for every token or product against Capital Rules s.361 and the CRP-1 guidance, including any treatment of permissionless blockchains, and confirm which group and risk weight apply.

**Set the appetite in the board risk statement:** Fix a hard Group 2 limit even though the statutory 1% ratio binds only G-SIBs and D-SIBs, with breach reporting and rectification steps. Record how the s.387 ratio and long and short positions are measured.

**Speak to the HKMA early:** Brief the supervisor before any holding or collateral programme starts. The research found no HKMA-specific rule on lending against crypto, so expect a case-by-case view and possible conditions.

**Fix the custody and key position:** Confirm who holds the keys, how assets are segregated, and how the bank reconciles on-chain balances. See the card on holding customers' virtual assets (custody) for the HKMA custody expectations.

**Build the collateral file:** If taking crypto as collateral, document haircuts, valuation feeds, liquidation rights on insolvency and perfection of security. The Basel standard is under targeted review, so do not rely on current treatment staying fixed.

**Update returns and disclosure:** Confirm the finance team can populate the new capital returns and the Pillar 3 crypto templates by the first reporting date, and that the Exposure Limits Code is reflected in policy.

**Check stablecoin holdings separately:** A licensed issuer's token still needs its own classification. The research found no confirmed rule giving licensed stablecoins automatic Group 1b treatment, so do not assume it.
watchFor: **Basel review pending:** In November 2025 the Basel Committee agreed to expedite a targeted review, including of permissionless blockchains, and in February 2026 said an update would follow later in 2026. Check the BCBS website for any revised standard. Treat today's rules as in force but movable.
**Hedging assumptions:** Group 2b gets no hedge recognition and Group 2a only limited recognition. A desk that models a fully hedged position can still face a full capital charge.

**Permissionless chains:** Group 1 treatment for a token on a permissionless blockchain depends on meeting and evidencing the s.361 conditions and CRP-1 guidance. An HKMA letter of 3 June 2026 clarified para 2.6.4 of CRP-1; check for any later clarification before relying on it.

**Secondary-source figures:** Some summaries describe the 1% and 2% Group 2 limit as applying to all AIs. Capital Rules s.388 confines it to G-SIBs and D-SIBs, so read the rule text, not summaries, before fixing limits.

activities.title: Running bank processes on blockchain or smart contracts
activities.summary: The bank wants to run internal or customer-facing processes, such as settlement, collateral movement or record-keeping, on distributed ledger technology or smart contracts. This changes the bank's technology, outsourcing and operational-resilience risk even if no customer holds a token.
activities.route: Yes. No separate licence is needed, because it is a way of running permitted banking business. The HKMA reviews DLT proposals against its April 2024 risk considerations, so brief it before launch and expect questions on governance, design and monitoring.
require: **Board responsibility:** The HKMA's April 2024 circular on DLT risk management says the board and senior management should take full responsibility for DLT adoption. The circular is non-statutory guidance, but it signals what the HKMA will test.

**Three review areas:** The HKMA looks at governance, application design and development, and ongoing maintenance and monitoring. Policies on technology risk, business continuity and outsourcing should be updated for DLT-specific factors.

**Key and cyber security:** The circular expects private-key security and cyber security at least commensurate with traditional applications. The HKMA's February 2024 custody guidance also addresses smart-contract security in custody arrangements.

**Operational resilience:** A DLT process that supports a critical operation falls within the HKMA's operational resilience module OR-2. AIs had until 31 May 2026 to implement their frameworks, including mapping and scenario testing.
**General conduct duty:** The MA must take reasonable steps to ensure business is carried on with prudence and competence (Cap. 155 s.7(2)(g)). Unmanaged DLT risk can feed into that assessment.

**Outsourcing:** If a node operator, wallet provider or platform vendor runs a function for the bank, the HKMA's outsourcing expectations in SPM SA-2 apply. Consult the HKMA before any material outsourcing.
gates: **Write the DLT business case and risk assessment:** Map the process, the chain type (permissioned or permissionless), the asset or data on-chain and the failure modes. Have the board or its delegated risk committee approve it.

**Brief the HKMA before build:** Describe the use case, chain choice and vendors to the relationship team. Ask whether the bank should use Project Ensemble or another pilot instead of building alone. Record the HKMA's feedback.
**Run an independent smart-contract audit:** Get a written audit and a remediation log before go-live. Define who can pause, upgrade or patch a contract, and how upgrades are approved.

**Settle key management:** Document key generation, storage, signing authority, rotation and recovery. Test recovery from loss or compromise. Confirm no single person can move assets or alter contract logic.
**Map OR-2 impacts:** Add the process to critical-operation mapping if it supports one, set impact tolerances, and run a scenario test, for example chain halt, node failure or an exploit.

**Paper the vendor contract:** Secure audit and access rights, incident notice, exit and data-return terms, and the HKMA's right to information. See the card on offering staking, DeFi access or crypto yield if the vendor touches public protocols.
**Check data and finality:** Confirm with legal when an on-chain entry is final, how errors are reversed on an immutable ledger, and how personal data is kept off-chain to satisfy PDPO duties.
watchFor: **Immutability against erasure:** Personal data written to a public chain cannot be corrected or deleted. Keep it off-chain or hash it, and test the design against PDPO retention and correction duties.
**Hidden outsourcing:** Using a third-party chain, oracle or node provider is outsourcing in substance. Do not treat open protocols as if no vendor existed.
**Pilot is not approval:** Taking part in an HKMA sandbox or Project Ensemble pilot does not clear the bank's own governance. The pilot is not law.
**Unread baseline modules:** The research did not confirm whether TM-G-1 or OR-2 contain DLT-specific paragraphs. Read both modules in full rather than relying on the 2024 circular alone.

activities.title: Running an e-wallet or prepaid balance
activities.summary: An e-wallet or prepaid balance lets customers store value with the bank and then pay or transfer from it. A bank is regarded as an SVF licensee, so the product is regulated inside the bank, with some licensee rules switched off for banks.
activities.route: Yes. Under Cap. 584 s.8G a licensed bank is regarded as holding an SVF licence from the grant of its banking licence, so no separate application is needed. Confirm that the product fits the [[stored value facility]] definition and that no partner becomes an unlicensed facilitator.
require: **Deemed licence:** Cap. 584 s.8G(a) treats a bank as holding an SVF licence from the time its banking licence is granted. Issuing or facilitating an SVF without that authority is an offence under s.8B, so the deemed licence is the bank's only authority.

**Safe and efficient operation:** Section 8O requires every licensee, banks included, to run each SVF safely and efficiently. Section 8P covers reliability, access control, information integrity and risk controls. Breach of s.8O is an offence. Section 8Q requires the applicable Sch. 3 minimum criteria to be met, though the principal-business, capital and fit-and-proper criteria do not apply to banks.

**Rules that do not apply to banks:** The licence fee (s.8M), reporting inability to meet obligations (s.8R), change-of-particulars notice (s.8S), MA intervention (Division 6) and controller consents (Division 7) are disapplied. A separate fee applies under s.8N, and Cap. 155 governs controllers and directors.

**Float rules still apply:** Section 8ZZZH on winding up does not apply to banks, but the Sch. 3 criteria on keeping float separate and protected, and on full redemption, have no bank carve-out. Confirm [[DPS]] treatment against Cap. 581 Sch. 1.

**Licence follows the banking licence:** The deemed SVF licence is revoked if the banking licence is revoked (s.8U) and suspended while it is suspended (s.8Y). During suspension the bank must stop issuing or facilitating SVF and receiving money for storage (s.8ZB(1)).

**AML/CFT:** The HKMA's separate AML/CFT guideline for SVF licensees (effective 1 June 2023) may also reach banks that issue SVF. Whether it or the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline for AIs governs a bank wallet, including [[CDD]] and monitoring, should be confirmed with the HKMA. Sch. 3 requires adequate AML/CFT controls.
gates: **Confirm the product is an SVF** and map every flow (top-up, peer transfer, merchant payment, cash-out) against the single-purpose definition in s.2A and the Sch. 8 exemptions before treating any balance as outside, or exempt from, the SVF licensing regime.

**Settle which AML/CFT guideline applies** to the wallet and record the HKMA's view. Do the same for the HKMA Guideline on Supervision of SVF Licensees, whose application to bank-deemed licensees was not confirmed.
**Agree the DPS and disclosure position** for wallet balances, and align customer terms and marketing with it, so customers understand how float protection differs from deposit protection.

**Review partner contracts** for facilitator risk under s.2B, where a non-issuer provides consideration that determines how much the issuer may undertake. Treat wallet, card and acquiring vendors as [[material outsourcing]] candidates.
**Wire in fraud controls** before launch: Scameter data, the FPS suspicious proxy ID and account alerts, mule-account detection, and an [[STR]] route to the [[JFIU]].
**Set limits and risk appetite** (balance caps, transaction limits, onboarding tiers) with board and risk sign-off, and brief the bank's HKMA supervisors before launch.
**Plan for suspension and exit** under s.8ZB(1), including how to stop issuance and return balances if the banking licence is suspended or the product is withdrawn.
watchFor: **Mule accounts:** Instant FPS top-ups and transfers make wallets attractive to mule networks. The HKMA, Police and banking industry have announced successive anti-fraud and mule-account measures, so expect scrutiny of detection and information sharing.

**Importing non-bank SVF packs wholesale:** Many licensee-only provisions are disapplied for banks, but s.8O and the Sch. 3 criteria without a bank carve-out still bite. Copying a non-bank licensee's compliance pack can over- or under-state what applies.
**Quoting market numbers:** Counts of non-bank SVF licensees conflict between sources. Only the HKMA register kept under s.8ZZZF is authoritative, so check it rather than quoting a number.

activities.title: Sending and receiving virtual-asset transfers, including unhosted wallets
activities.summary: Customers may want to move virtual assets to or from the bank, other institutions and wallets they control themselves (unhosted wallets). Such transfers raise sanctions, fraud and money-laundering risk and attract a statutory travel rule that applies to banks.
activities.route: Yes in principle. AMLO Sch. 2 s.13A applies the travel rule to financial institutions, including AIs, that carry out virtual asset transfers, and the rule itself needs no extra licence. Holding or dealing in assets for customers follows the routes in "Holding customers' virtual assets (custody)" and "Buying and selling virtual assets for customers".
require: **Ordering institution:** Before transferring, the bank must obtain and record the originator's name, account number or unique reference, and address, ID number or date and place of birth, plus the recipient's name and account number or reference. It must send this to the beneficiary institution (Sch. 2 s.13A(2), (4)).

**HK$8,000 threshold:** Where the virtual assets are worth less than HK$8,000, the originator address, ID and birth data are not required and are not sent (s.13A(3), (4)(b)). The other items still apply, so the bank needs a pricing and linked-transaction rule.

**Beneficiary and intermediary roles:** A beneficiary institution must obtain and record the information (s.13A(5)). An intermediary institution must pass on all the information it receives (s.13A(6)).

**Missing or meaningless data:** Under s.13A(7) the bank must obtain missing information as soon as reasonably practicable. If it cannot, it must consider restricting or ending the relationship with the instructing institution, or take reasonable risk-mitigation measures.

**CDD for occasional transfers:** The HKMA AML/CFT Guideline for AIs (May 2023) para 4.2.1(b)(iii) requires [[CDD]] before an occasional virtual asset transfer of no less than HK$8,000. Footnote 15 points to s.13A. A customer with an account booked in Hong Kong is not an occasional case.

**SFC guideline for registered institutions:** Footnote 1 of the HKMA guideline tells AIs that are [[registered institutions|registered institution]] or associated entities to have regard to the SFC AML/CFT Guideline, including Chapter 12 on virtual assets.
gates: **Fix the product scope** (send-only, receive-only, hosted-to-hosted, or customer-to-unhosted) and confirm the bank never takes possession of client assets without the custody route. Confirm the design cannot amount to operating a VA exchange under Part 5B (s.53ZRD offence; Sch. 3B).
**Choose a travel-rule solution** and test it end to end. It must identify whether the counterparty is a regulated institution, carry the required data, and log what was sent and received.
**Run counterparty due diligence** on every institution the bank exchanges data with, and document the escalation path for counterparties that cannot or will not supply information.

**Write an unhosted-wallet policy** covering ownership confirmation, limits, enhanced review, or prohibition. Check the SFC guideline's Chapter 12 text itself before copying any approach, as secondary summaries of its paragraph numbering were not verified.
**Define the HK$8,000 test**, covering the price source, valuation time and treatment of linked transfers, approved by compliance and built into the transfer engine.

**Screen addresses and transfers** with blockchain analytics and sanctions tools, and set clear hold, reject and return rules, with an [[STR]] route to the [[JFIU]] when information is missing or suspicious.
**Brief the HKMA and obtain board and risk sign-off** before first release, with an agreed list of transfer types, jurisdictions and counterparties in scope.
watchFor: **Threshold splitting:** Customers can split transfers to stay under HK$8,000. A linked-transaction rule and monitoring for structuring are needed, not just a single-transaction check.

**Self-declared wallet control:** A customer's statement that a wallet is theirs is not proof. Secondary reports describe the SFC guideline as expecting ownership confirmation, such as a test transfer, but that text should be checked before relying on it.
**Fake and unverified stablecoins:** The HKMA has warned about fake tokens claiming links to licensed stablecoin issuers. Do not credit or release tokens without verifying the issuer.
**Drift into custody:** Receiving assets into bank-controlled wallets, even briefly, may be custody. Treat it under "Holding customers' virtual assets (custody)" before launch.

activities.title: Banking VASPs, trading platforms and stablecoin issuers
activities.summary: VASPs, trading platforms and stablecoin issuers need bank accounts for operations, settlement and client money flows. They are higher-risk customers, yet the HKMA has encouraged a risk-based approach to legitimate businesses rather than blanket refusal.
activities.route: Yes. Providing accounts to these customers needs no extra licence, but the bank must apply risk-based [[CDD]] and, for correspondent-type services to VASPs outside Hong Kong, should apply the correspondent-banking additional measures. Reserve accounts for issuers are covered in "Banking for stablecoin issuers: reserve accounts and custody of reserves".
require: **Licensing status of the customer:** Operating a VA exchange, or holding out as doing so, without an SFC licence is an offence under Cap. 615 s.53ZRD (Part 5B). The bank should confirm that a platform customer is licensed or has a defensible basis for being unlicensed.

**Stablecoin issuers:** Carrying on a regulated stablecoin activity without a licence is an offence under Cap. 656 s.8, and ss.10 and 11 cover advertising and fraud. A banking licence does not authorize issuance. The first licences took effect on 10 April 2026.

**Correspondent-type services:** Paras 11.23-11.25 of the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline apply the additional correspondent measures to services for VASPs outside Hong Kong. The bank should ascertain whether the account is for the customer's own purposes or to serve its clients, and could encourage two separate accounts.

**Proportionate access:** An HKMA circular of 27 April 2023, "Access to Banking Services for Corporate Customers", urged banks to take a proportionate risk-based approach, avoid wholesale de-risking and support licensed VASPs' legitimate need for accounts.

**Ongoing duties:** Standard CDD, ongoing monitoring and [[STR]] reporting to the [[JFIU]] apply. Fn 79 of the guideline says the correspondent extension does not apply to an institution that is a financial institution as defined in the AMLO.

**Information sharing:** Banking Ordinance Part XIIAA (ss.68AA-68AAM) (in force since 3 November 2025) allows AIs to share suspected money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing information on HKMA-designated platforms without customer consent. Platform access needs MA approval (s.68AAH).
gates: **Adopt a board-approved acceptance policy** that separates SFC-licensed platforms, overseas VASPs, licensed stablecoin issuers and unlicensed or applicant businesses, and states which products each may receive.
**Verify and re-verify licence status** against the SFC and HKMA registers at onboarding and on a set cycle. Require the customer to notify any change, suspension or condition by contract.
**Require account segregation** where the customer both trades for itself and holds client funds. Agree in advance which accounts hold client money and which hold house funds.
**Calibrate monitoring** for flows to and from VASPs, including blockchain-analytics alerts, [[money mule]] typologies and [[Scameter]] data, and test the rules against known scam patterns.
**Document exit and escalation** steps, so that restricting or ending a relationship follows a recorded risk decision, not a reflex, and customers receive consistent treatment.
**Confirm Part XIIAA access** and internal approvals before relying on information sharing, and align privacy notices and PDPO assessments with it.
**Talk to the HKMA early** about appetite and any customer types the bank plans to exclude, and record the board and risk sign-off.
watchFor: **Two opposite errors:** Wholesale de-risking can conflict with the HKMA's stated expectations, while wholesale acceptance ignores the customers' risk profile. The file should show a reasoned, customer-specific decision.

**Fake and lookalike tokens:** The HKMA has warned about fake tokens claiming links to licensed issuers. Customers claiming to be issuers or their agents should be checked against the licensed issuer register.
**Nested exposure:** A VASP's own customers and sub-accounts sit behind the account. Without clear understanding of its customer base, the bank can carry risk it did not underwrite.
**Quoting licensee counts:** Figures for licensed trading platforms came from a single secondary article. Check the SFC register for the current list instead of repeating a number.

activities.title: Funding P2P platforms and money lenders
activities.summary: The bank lends to, or takes security over loan books of, licensed money lenders, P2P platforms and similar non-bank credit providers. It matters because the bank's credit and conduct risk now rests on a borrower whose own licence status and lending terms can make its loans unenforceable.
activities.route: Yes. Lending to a money lender is ordinary banking business and the bank needs no money lender licence, because the Money Lenders Ordinance (MLO) does not apply to an authorized institution. Diligence must test the counterparty's own licence, exemption and lending terms.
require: **Bank exemption:** The MLO does not apply to an [[authorized institution]] (s.3(a)), nor to a person who lends to one (s.3(b)). Funding a platform therefore needs no bank-side licence, but the borrower's position is tested separately.

**Borrower must be licensed or exempt:** Carrying on a money lending business without a licence, away from licensed premises or outside licence conditions is an offence (ss.7(1), 29(1), 32(1)(a)). A breach of a licence condition is itself an offence.

**Business test:** A person is a money lender if lending is its business or it holds itself out as lending (s.2(1)). A platform that lends, or advertises as lender, is caught unless Sch. 1 excludes it.

**Rate limits:** Lending above 48% effective rate is an offence and the agreement and security are unenforceable (s.24). A rate above 36% is presumed extortionate and a court may reopen the loan (s.25(3)).

**Enforceability:** A lender cannot recover through the courts unless licensed when it made the loan, subject to an equitable discretion (s.23). Agreements must also meet the s.18 formalities and the s.22 restrictions.

**Licence conditions:** Licences carry conditions imposed under s.11(6), published by the Registrar, covering matters such as third-party referrals, personal data sourcing and debt collection. Serious breach can lead the licensing court to suspend or revoke the licence (s.14(1)).
gates: **Verify the borrower's status** on the Registrar's public register (ss.4, 6) at onboarding and on each drawdown, and record the licence number, premises and conditions in the credit file.

**Test every exemption claimed** against Sch. 1. A subsidiary of an AI (Pt 1 para 1), a Pt 2 para 12 loan to a company with HK$1,000,000 paid-up capital, and the Pt 2 para 5 non-primary-lender exemption are each fact-sensitive and should be evidenced.

**Add licence covenants** to the facility. Require continuing licence, compliance with conditions and the rate limits, prompt notice of suspension, revocation or Registrar action, and audit rights over loan files.

**Diligence the loan book** before taking security or buying receivables. Sample agreements for s.18 formalities, rates above 36% and 48%, s.27 charges to borrowers and compound or default-rate clauses that s.22 makes illegal.

**Check the data chain.** Confirm how the lender sourced borrower data and that it can evidence lawful collection as its licence conditions expect. Add PDPO warranties before any transfer of borrower data to the bank.

**Cover the collection risk.** Require the lender and its collectors to follow the licensing conditions on harassment and records. Agree a step-in or termination right if complaints rise, since reputational loss falls on the funder.

**Obtain credit-committee and risk sign-off** on concentration, counterparty rating and the legal opinion on enforceability. Brief the HKMA relationship manager where the exposure is large or the model is novel.
watchFor: **Unlicensed arrangements:** A platform that says it only 'matches' but sets terms, holds funds or advertises as lender may be a money lender in substance. Look at conduct, not the contract label.
**Pooled investor money:** If the platform raises money from retail investors, the structure may engage the SFO as well. See the card on running a P2P lending marketplace.
**Stale status checks:** Licences last 12 months (s.12) and can be suspended. A one-off check at onboarding does not support continuing reliance.
**Reopening risk:** Extortionate-rate reopening applies to any person suing on the loan (s.25(1)), so a bank enforcing assigned loans can face the defence itself.

activities.title: Originating bank loans through platforms and buy-now-pay-later partners
activities.summary: The bank makes loans on its own balance sheet to customers introduced or served through a platform or a buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) partner. It matters because the bank keeps full conduct and credit responsibility for a journey that a third party designs and runs.
activities.route: Yes, as the lender, without a money lender licence. A bank's own BNPL and platform loans are supervised by the HKMA as consumer credit. A non-bank partner that itself makes loans needs a money lender licence.
require: **No MLO licence for the bank:** The MLO does not apply to an [[authorized institution]] (s.3(a)). A subsidiary of an AI is an exempted person (Sch. 1 Pt 1 para 1), so group structure matters if lending sits outside the bank.

**Government position:** The Government has said in LegCo replies that bank BNPL is supervised by the HKMA, while non-bank BNPL providers that make loans need a money lender licence. No dedicated BNPL statute was found.

**Rate limits through the Code:** The [[Code of Banking Practice]] expects bank lending rates to stay within the MLO benchmarks. An HKMA circular of 27 October 2022 asked AIs to reflect the revised 48% and 36% limits, which took effect on 30 December 2022.

**BNPL consumer protection:** An HKMA circular of 2 September 2022 set consumer-protection measures for bank BNPL. Banks must label it as credit, show a "borrow only if you can repay" message, explain chargeback arrangements and assess repayment ability. Banks answer for third-party partners, with implementation by end-2022.

**Cooling-off:** An HKMA circular of November 2024 expects retail banks, including digital banks, to give at least 7 calendar days' cooling-off from drawdown on unsecured consumer credit for individuals, with compliance by end-June 2025. The exact circular day was not confirmed.

**Outsourcing and collection:** The bank stays responsible for outsourced functions under SA-2 and for third-party collection under the Code. SA-2 expects the bank to discuss material outsourcing with the HKMA in advance.
gates: **Decide who is the lender of record.** Document that the bank, not the partner, makes and holds the loan, and that the partner is an agent or service provider only. If the partner also lends, confirm its licence or Sch. 1 exemption.

**Classify the arrangement** as [[material outsourcing]] or not, and record the reasoning. If material, plan the advance discussion with the HKMA before launch and set up exit, audit and business-continuity rights in the contract.

**Map the customer journey** against the HKMA's BNPL measures and any cooling-off expectation. Obtain evidence that screens, disclosures and chargeback terms are the bank's, and approved by compliance.

**Own the credit decision.** Keep scoring, affordability and approval under the bank's policy. If using alternative data, check it against the HKMA's personal-lending credit risk circulars and consider [[Credit Data Smart]] and credit reference agency use.
**Control the data flows.** Review PDPO notices, the PCPD Code of Practice on Consumer Credit Data and partner sub-processing. Limit what the partner may keep, reuse or share with other lenders.
**Cap the fees.** Make sure no fee charged to the borrower, by bank or partner, pushes the effective rate past the Code limits, and check how referral fees paid to the partner are disclosed.
**Obtain board or risk committee approval** with stress tests for default and fraud, and confirm complaint handling, collection standards and termination triggers in the partner contract.
watchFor: **Partner as hidden lender:** If the partner funds or sells any part of the loan, or holds itself out as lender, it may be a money lender. Its advertising must also carry the licence number (s.26). See the card on Funding P2P platforms and money lenders.
**Delegated collection:** Passing referee or third-party data to collectors, or tolerating harassment, breaches the Code and the HKMA's long-standing expectations on collection agencies.
**Marketing as credit:** BNPL branded as 'interest-free' or 'pay later' without credit labelling is a conduct risk even where the APR is nil.
**Weak sources:** The BNPL, cooling-off and personal-lending circular points rest partly on secondary summaries. Check the primary circulars before relying on thresholds.

activities.title: Running a P2P lending marketplace
activities.summary: The bank, or a group company, operates a platform that matches investors or lenders with borrowers, possibly pooling money or issuing loan participations. It matters because the structure can fall under the money lender regime, the securities regime or both, and Hong Kong has no dedicated P2P statute.
activities.route: Not as a plain banking product. The route depends on structure: the platform may need a money lender licence, SFC authorization or an exemption for offers to the public, and SFC registration for any regulated activity. Raise the model with the HKMA and SFC before design is fixed.
require: **No dedicated regime:** The Government has said some P2P lending may fall under the SFO and that lenders need a money lender licence (LegCo reply, 2017). The 19 December 2022 crowdfunding consultation is a proposal, and no outcome or legislation was found.

**SFO engagement:** The SFC's 7 May 2014 crowdfunding notice says P2P lending may be a collective investment scheme or involve securities, depending on structure. Pooled funds and loan participations are the main risk.

**Public offers:** SFO s.103 restricts advertisements and invitations to the public to acquire securities or join a collective investment scheme unless the SFC authorizes them or an exemption applies. Section 104 allows authorization of schemes and s.105 authorization of the advertisements themselves.
**Regulated activity:** SFO s.114 bars carrying on a regulated activity business without a licence or registration. An AI doing so must be an SFC [[registered institution]] (s.119).

**MLO if the platform lends:** A platform that makes loans or holds itself out as lender is a money lender (s.2(1)) and needs a licence unless excluded. Its advertising must show the licence number (s.26). See the card on Funding P2P platforms and money lenders.

**Borrower-side limits:** Any loan made through the marketplace is subject to the 48% rate cap (s.24), the 36% extortionate presumption (s.25(3)) and the ban on charging borrowers arranging costs (s.27).
gates: **Fix the legal structure first.** Decide who lends, who holds the loan, and what investors receive. Document whether each investor gets a direct loan, a participation, a note or a unit, and obtain a written classification opinion.

**Resolve the SFO position.** Confirm whether the product is a collective investment scheme or securities and which Types of regulated activity are engaged. Check the Sch. 1 and Sch. 5 definitions directly, as the local text was not available.

**Settle the licence route.** Confirm the bank's registered-institution scope covers the activity, or that a separate licensed entity runs the platform. A group lender may use the AI-subsidiary exemption in Sch. 1 Pt 1 para 1 only if the entity qualifies.

**Hold a pre-launch conversation** with the HKMA and SFC. Present the structure, investor class, disclosures and exit plan. Treat the conversation as a gate, since no published P2P guidance exists to rely on.

**Design investor protection.** Draft risk disclosure, suitability or eligibility rules, segregation of client money, default and secondary-market rules, and advertising approval that satisfies s.103 and the MLO licence-number rule.

**Check money flows and AML.** Apply [[CDD]] to investors and borrowers, handle pooled accounts, and set out how repayments are collected and passed on. Include platform-failure and wind-down arrangements.
**Obtain board approval** with a documented risk appetite, since the activity falls outside ordinary deposit and lending business and may carry reputational and enforcement exposure.
watchFor: **Label risk:** Calling the platform a 'marketplace' or the product a 'loan' does not take it outside the SFO or the MLO. The SFC and courts look at substance.
**Retail marketing:** Promotions to the public that describe returns can breach s.103 even if the underlying loans are lawful. Clear all copy with the SFC position in mind.
**Borrower fees:** Origination or introduction fees charged to borrowers on a licensed lender's loans need care under s.27 and may count as interest for the 48% test.
**Old authority:** The SFC notice is from 2014 and the Government reply from 2017. No later P2P-specific statement was found, so confirm the current view directly with the regulators.

activities.title: Offering staking, DeFi access or crypto yield
activities.summary: Staking lets a customer earn rewards by locking proof-of-stake tokens; DeFi access and crypto yield products route customer assets into lending pools, liquidity pools or similar protocols. Each adds custody, smart-contract, counterparty and deposit-mischaracterisation risk that a bank must price before launch.
activities.route: Only staking as an add-on to an approved custody or VA-dealing service is a defined route: the bank should discuss it with the HKMA first and follow the April 2025 staking circular. Direct DeFi access or a deposit-like crypto yield product has no approved route and should not be launched on current guidance.
require: **Staking circular:** The HKMA's 7 April 2025 circular sets expectations for AIs that stake as part of custody. The bank should keep control of withdrawal mechanisms, safeguard against errors and misconduct, disclose fees, lock-ups and risks, and talk to the HKMA before launch.

**Base framework:** Dealing in or advising on VAs by an AI or registered institution runs under the HKMA and SFC joint circular of 22 December 2023 as supplemented on 30 September 2025, which allows staking on conditions. Check the current version for the staking terms.

**Custody first:** Staking presupposes holding the customer's tokens. The HKMA's February 2024 custody circular applies to the underlying custody, and the bank should treat staking as an extension of that approval, not a separate product.

**Licensing line:** A bank is not a licensed VATP. SFC circular 25EC22 (7 April 2025) lets licensed VATPs stake on conditions. The SFC's revised authorised-funds circular of that day lets funds stake only through licensed VATPs and AIs, subject to a cap. Check the text before acting as staking agent.

**Deposit label:** Staked tokens are not deposits and are not DPS-protected. Cap. 155 s.92 restricts deposit advertising but exempts invitations to deposit with an AI, so for a bank the main risk of a deposit-style label is misdescription and mis-selling.

**DeFi under SFO:** The SFC has issued no dedicated DeFi circular. Secondary reports of SFC speeches say that DeFi activity within the SFO scope is regulated like traditional activity, so a protocol trading securities or futures can need licensing. Treat that as direction of travel, not a safe harbour.
gates: **Confirm the product class** by deciding whether the offer is native-token staking through custody, a pooled or liquid-staking product, or DeFi lending. Only the first has a defined regulatory route; escalate the others to the HKMA before design work continues.

**Obtain HKMA engagement** in writing before launch, covering validators, key control, slashing risk, unbonding periods and who bears loss. Keep the correspondence on the file as evidence of the consultation the circular expects.

**Settle the contract terms** so that the customer knows lock-up periods, reward variability, fees, slashing allocation and the right to unstake. Reward promises that look like fixed interest should be reviewed against the deposit-advertising offence.

**Diligence validators and protocols** as third parties, with a material outsourcing review where relevant, smart-contract audit evidence, exit rights and a tested unwind plan. Link these to the vendor clause themes on audit, sub-contracting and termination assistance.

**Segregate and reconcile** staked assets from the bank's own, test that the bank can always evidence ownership and withdraw, and settle how client assets are treated on insolvency. Contract terms drive client-asset outcomes in disputes over crypto holdings.

**Run product governance** through the new-product committee with suitability or target-market rules for retail customers, a risk-disclosure document, and board or risk sign-off on capital treatment of any crypto exposure the bank keeps. See Holding crypto-assets or taking them as collateral on the bank's balance sheet.
**Check marketing copy** against Cap. 155 s.92, Cap. 615 s.53ZRE and the SFO promotion rules, and ensure no document describes a third-party DeFi protocol as bank-guaranteed or DPS-protected.
watchFor: **Yield dressed as deposits:** Marketing that promises an annual percentage return on crypto held with the bank invites HKMA challenge and a mis-selling complaint. Do not use savings or deposit language for non-deposit products.

**Unlicensed counterparties:** Routing customer tokens to an overseas staking provider or protocol that markets to Hong Kong may itself breach the VA licensing rules, and active marketing to the public is deemed to be carrying on business (Cap. 615 s.53ZRB). Confirm the provider's status.
**Slashing and smart-contract loss:** Staked assets can be penalised or drained through protocol failure. The loss falls on the customer only if the terms say so clearly and the disclosure was fair.

**Moving rules:** Circular references and the proposed VA dealing and custody licensing regimes are still moving. SFC circulars addressed to licensed VATPs do not apply to banks, so do not import them by analogy. Re-check status before each release.

activities.title: NFTs, loyalty tokens and Web3 marketing
activities.summary: A bank may want to issue or sell NFTs, run a tokenised loyalty scheme, or promote itself in the metaverse and Web3 communities. Whether the token is a virtual asset, a security, an SVF or an unregulated collectible decides which regime applies.
activities.route: Yes for a closed, non-convertible loyalty token that meets the limited-purpose test and for ordinary Web3 marketing that follows general advertising rules. A tradeable or cash-convertible token, or an NFT structured as fractional interests, needs classification advice first and may bring SFC, SVF or VA rules into play.
require: **VA definition:** A token that is a cryptographically secured digital representation of value used as a medium of exchange accepted by the public, or giving governance voting rights over one, is a VA (Cap. 615 s.53ZRA(1)). Securities, futures contracts, SVF float and limited-purpose tokens are excluded (s.53ZRA(2)).

**Loyalty carve-out:** A limited purpose digital token is excluded from VA (Cap. 615 s.53ZRA(2)). Section 53ZR covers loyalty or reward points, in-game assets, and similar tokens the issuer does not intend to be convertible into money or another public medium of exchange.

**NFT classification:** The SFC said on 6 June 2022 that unique collectible NFTs are mostly outside its remit. NFTs structured as fractional or fungible interests, or as collective investment scheme interests, may be securities, and marketing them can need SFC licensing or authorization.

**SVF line:** Knowingly promoting or assisting another person to issue an SVF without a licence is an offence (Cap. 584 s.8C). A bank co-marketing a partner's token that is in fact multi-purpose and convertible risks this.

**Advertising:** Active marketing of VA services to the public is deemed to be carrying on that business, wherever it is done from (Cap. 615 s.53ZRB). Advertising an unlicensed VA service, knowing it is unlicensed, is an offence (s.53ZRE). Stablecoin promotions have a parallel offence (Cap. 656 s.10).

**Bank name:** Using the word bank, or implying banking business, without being a bank is an offence (Cap. 155 s.97). The HKMA issued an alert on misuse of the word in November 2024. A bank-branded token should not suggest a deposit.
gates: **Classify every token** in a written memo that tests it against the VA definition, the limited-purpose conditions, SFO securities and CIS definitions, and the SVF definition. Record the facts relied on, such as transferability, resale and convertibility.

**Lock the loyalty design** so points cannot be sold for cash, exchanged for other tokens or listed on a marketplace. Any secondary market or redemption for currency should send the design back to classification.

**Review partner terms** for who issues, who holds reserves, who handles customer funds and who carries regulatory risk. Add warranties on licensing status, indemnities and a termination right if the partner's token changes character.

**Clear the marketing plan** with compliance for each channel, including metaverse venues, social posts and influencer promotions. Check content against Cap. 155 s.92, Cap. 615 s.53ZRE, the Code of Banking Practice and, for securities-like products, SFO promotion rules.

**Run a data protection review** under the PDPO, especially where wallets, biometrics or on-chain identifiers are collected. Immutable ledgers conflict with data minimisation and retention duties (Sch. 1 DPP1 and DPP2), so keep personal data off-chain.

**Confirm legal form of any on-chain terms** because electronic contracts are valid in principle (Cap. 553 s.17), and ss.5 and 6 let electronic records and signatures meet writing and signature rules on conditions, but whether bare code qualifies is untested. Pair any smart-contract terms with conventional written terms and a governing-law clause.
**Obtain sign-off** from the new-product committee and the HKMA relationship team where the activity touches VAs, and keep a decision log on why the token falls outside each regime.
watchFor: **Convertibility creep:** A loyalty token that begins as closed can drift into a VA or SVF if the bank or partner later allows trading or cash-out. Build a change-control trigger for any redesign.

**DAO and governance tokens:** A governance token giving votes over another VA's arrangements can itself be a VA (Cap. 615 s.53ZRA(1)(a)(ii)(B)). Our reading is that DAO membership tokens may be caught unless they are securities; no regulator statement has been found.

**Biometric wallets:** A PCPD enforcement notice of 22 May 2024 directed Worldcoin to stop scanning iris and face images in Hong Kong. It shows how Web3 projects collecting such data can breach the PDPO. Treat biometric onboarding to a wallet as high risk.

**Gaps in guidance:** No HKMA or SFC circular on bank marketing in the metaverse was found, and the NFT statement may have been updated since 2022. Re-check before launch rather than assuming the 2022 position stands.

title: Supervision & enforcement
oneLiner: Most HKMA pressure is private and continuous; knowing the statutory powers behind it shapes every regulatory conversation.
keyPoints: Authorization starts the relationship with the HKMA; it does not end it. The HKMA supervises continuously and on a risk basis.

**Methods:** It rates every institution under its [[CAMEL rating]] system, combines off-site review of returns and management information with [[on-site examinations|on-site examination]] and thematic reviews, and meets boards, management and auditors regularly.

**Banking Ordinance:** gives the Monetary Authority (MA) information and inspection powers, a ladder of intervention powers for when things go wrong (directions, an [[Advisor]], a [[Manager]], suspension, revocation) and criminal offences for serious misconduct.
**AMLO:** The Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance adds a separate disciplinary regime with fines.
**Secrecy:** Statutory secrecy keeps most supervisory dealings private, so the enforcement the public sees is only a small part of the picture.
**Counsel's role:** Keep the relationship candid, timely and well documented.

deepDive.heading: Continuous, risk-based supervision
deepDive.lede: Supervision is continuous and mostly private.

visual.caption: Ratings and findings are confidential supervisory information.

items.label: Risk assessment
items.note: Eight inherent risks and the quality of risk management

items.label: The supervisory cycle
items.note: Off-site analysis, examinations, prudential and tripartite meetings

points: **SA-1:** The HKMA assesses eight inherent risks and the quality of risk management, and integrates the results with its CAMEL rating.
**Supervisory intensity:** The rating sets how intensively the bank is supervised.

**Supervisory cycle:** Off-site analysis alternates with full-scope or thematic examinations, prudential meetings with management, and [[tripartite meetings|tripartite meeting]] with the external auditor.
**Confidentiality:** Ratings and findings are confidential supervisory information, so ask for the HKMA's view before repeating them to investors, parents or vendors.

deepDive.heading: Information and examination powers
deepDive.lede: The hard powers sit in the Ordinance.
points: **s.63:** underpins returns and ad hoc information requests.
**s.55:** underpins examinations.
**Section 59 reports:** under s.59(2) the MA can require a report from an auditor it has approved under s.59(3) (a [[section 59 report]]), the HKMA's equivalent of a skilled-person review.
**Auditor channels:** The bank's own auditor also has statutory reporting channels to the MA, so align with the auditor early.
**False information:** Individuals who give the MA materially false information can be prosecuted.

deepDive.heading: Escalation and appeals
deepDive.lede: Escalation usually starts with a findings letter and a remediation plan with deadlines.
points: **Directions and appointments:** Beyond that, s.52 lets the MA direct specific action, require the bank to consult an Advisor, or appoint a Manager.
**End points:** revocation (s.22, on [[Eighth Schedule]] grounds, after notice and a hearing under s.23) and suspension (ss.24–25).
**Appeals:** Appeals against many MA decisions go to the Chief Executive in Council; capital, liquidity and disclosure decisions go to the [[Banking Review Tribunal]].
**AML track:** AML breaches follow a separate track: under AMLO s.21 the HKMA can issue public reprimands, remedial orders and fines.
**Published enforcement:** This is where most published HKMA enforcement appears.

items.label: Findings letter
items.note: With a remediation plan and deadlines

items.label: s.52 powers
items.note: Direct specific action, require an Advisor, or appoint a Manager

items.label: Revocation or suspension
items.note: Revocation on Eighth Schedule grounds, after notice and a hearing

deepDive.heading: Working with the HKMA
deepDive.lede: For counsel, 'no surprises' is the working rule.
points: **Early reporting:** Report significant incidents and breaches early, with the known facts and a plan, and confirm every oral briefing in writing.
**Investigations:** Commission investigations through counsel, and give the HKMA facts, chronology and remediation rather than legal advice.
**Privileged reports:** If one must be produced, use express limited-waiver terms, accepting that protection against third parties is not guaranteed.
**s.120:** binds the HKMA, not the bank. It keeps supervisory files out of public view but does not make the bank's own documents privileged.
deepDive.takeaway: Contest examination findings on the facts, in writing, before the report is finalised.

provisions.title: Risk-based supervisory approach and CAMEL
provisions.summary: Describes the HKMA's risk-based supervision (V.2, 23 December 2022). It assesses eight types of inherent risk (credit, market, interest rate, liquidity, operational, reputation, legal and strategic) and the quality of risk management, integrates the results with the CAMEL rating system, and runs a cycle of off-site reviews, on-site examinations and meetings with the institution. The 2022 revision expects emerging risks, such as climate risk, to be considered within the eight inherent risks.
provisions.counselNote: This module explains why the HKMA asks what it asks. The CAMEL composite rating drives how intensively the bank is supervised and is confidential supervisory information.

provisions.title: Returns and information to the MA
provisions.summary: Requires AIs to submit periodic returns to the MA. s.63(2) also supports requests for further information the MA reasonably needs (HKMA forms such as the annual compliance certificate cite it as their legal basis). Non-compliance carries criminal sanctions.
provisions.counselNote: Every regulatory return and ad hoc HKMA data request rests on this section. Errors in returns are regulatory events in their own right, so treat their accuracy and sign-off controls as legal controls.

provisions.title: Examination of AIs
provisions.summary: Empowers the MA to examine an AI's books, accounts and transactions. The HKMA relies on this power for on-site examinations and thematic reviews, and information obtained this way is protected by statutory secrecy.
provisions.counselNote: Requests made during an examination are compulsory, not voluntary. Manage document production, interviews and responses to draft findings as you would a formal regulatory process.

provisions.title: Auditor reports required by the MA
provisions.summary: Under s.59(2) the MA may by notice require an AI to submit a report by an auditor on matters the MA reasonably requires for its functions; under s.59(3) the auditor must be approved by the MA. Published examples include reports on Bank of China (Hong Kong) in 2003 and Octopus Cards Limited in 2010.
provisions.counselNote: A s.59 report is the HKMA's 'skilled person' tool, often used after incidents or to validate remediation. Negotiate the scope and terms of reference carefully, because the report goes to the regulator. Separately, the bank's own auditor has statutory duties to report certain significant matters to the MA.

provisions.title: Remedial powers: directions, Advisor, Manager
provisions.summary: On statutory grounds that broadly cover actual or likely inability to meet obligations, conduct detrimental to depositors' interests and contraventions of the Ordinance, the MA may direct an AI to take specified action (s.52(1)(A)), require it to seek advice from an Advisor (s.52(1)(B)), or place the management of its affairs, business and property with a Manager (s.52(1)(C)).
provisions.counselNote: These are the HKMA's main intervention tools short of revocation; past examples include an Advisor direction for Octopus Cards Limited and a Manager for Delta Asia Credit Limited. Directions restricting new business or requiring management changes are the realistic escalation for a struggling digital bank.

provisions.title: Revocation, suspension and appeals
provisions.summary: s.22 allows the MA to revoke an authorization on grounds listed in the Eighth Schedule, after informing the AI of the grounds and giving it an opportunity to be heard (s.23). s.24 provides for temporary suspension and s.25 for suspension. s.132A provides appeals to the Chief Executive in Council against specified MA decisions; decisions on capital, liquidity and disclosure requirements are instead reviewable by the Banking Review Tribunal.
provisions.counselNote: Revocation is the last resort, but its grounds (the HKMA treats the authorization criteria as continuing to apply after authorization) frame every serious supervisory conversation. Diarise appeal time limits as soon as any adverse decision is notified.

provisions.title: Official secrecy
provisions.summary: Prohibits the MA and persons performing functions under the Ordinance from disclosing information about any person's affairs obtained in that capacity, subject to listed exceptions (gateways) such as disclosure to other regulators in defined circumstances.
provisions.counselNote: This explains why the HKMA will not discuss peers and why examination reports are not public. It binds the HKMA, not the bank, and does not make the bank's own documents privileged.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Disciplinary action by relevant authorities
provisions.summary: Where a financial institution contravenes specified requirements (including the Schedule 2 customer due diligence and record-keeping requirements), the relevant authority, which for AIs is the HKMA, may publicly reprimand it, order remedial action, and impose a pecuniary penalty of up to the greater of HK$10 million or three times the profit gained or costs avoided.
provisions.counselNote: Most of the HKMA's public enforcement actions against banks are taken under this power. Read the HKMA's published guideline on exercising the pecuniary penalty power for the factors that aggravate or mitigate a penalty.

provisions.title: Criminal offences counsel should know
provisions.summary: Offences include issuing deposit advertisements other than by an AI, subject to exceptions (s.92), using 'bank' in a name without being a licensed bank or the MA's consent (s.97), holding out as a bank (s.97A), staff making false entries in an AI's records (s.123), and directors or employees accepting advantages for showing favour in granting credit (s.124). The Ordinance also penalises producing information that is false in a material particular; in January 2009 the District Court fined individuals for Banking Ordinance offences including this one.
provisions.counselNote: ss.123 and 124 apply to staff conduct and belong in training and the code of conduct. The false-information offences matter personally for anyone who signs returns or HKMA responses.

provisions.instrument: HKMA circular: Management Accountability at Registered Institutions
provisions.title: Senior management accountability (MIC-aligned)
provisions.summary: Sets HKMA expectations, in FAQ form, for senior management accountability over securities (regulated) activities at registered institutions, aligned with the SFC's Manager-in-Charge regime. 'Management' covers chief executives, alternate chief executives, directors approved under s.71 of the Banking Ordinance, managers under s.72B, executive officers approved under s.71C, and other persons involved in management.
provisions.counselNote: This becomes relevant if the digital bank registers to distribute investment products. Map responsible individuals and reporting lines, and keep s.71 approvals, s.72B manager notifications and executive officer approvals current.

checklist: **Map every regulatory return** to its data sources, owner and sign-off, and treat return errors as reportable events.
**Set up a single regulatory correspondence log** and point-of-contact protocol so that every HKMA request and response passes through legal or compliance.
**Prepare an examination playbook** covering a document request tracker, interviewee briefings and a factual-accuracy review step for draft findings.
**Agree a board-approved self-reporting policy** with thresholds, timelines and decision owners ('no surprises').
**Track every HKMA finding to closure** with root cause, owner, deadline and evidence, and report progress to the board.
**Protect privilege** by engaging investigators through counsel, separating factual chronologies from legal advice, and using limited-waiver terms when production is unavoidable.
**Brief approved individuals** (chief executive, alternate chief executives, directors and any executive officers) on their personal exposure under the Banking Ordinance and AMLO.
**Negotiate the terms of reference** for any s.59 engagement, covering scope, access, timetable and the bank's opportunity to comment on the draft report.
itAngle: **Data lineage:** Regulatory returns are data pipelines. Errors in source systems, transformations or reporting logic become s.63 issues, so data lineage, reconciliations and change control over reporting code are compliance controls.

**System evidence:** Examinations increasingly ask for system evidence such as access logs, configuration baselines, change tickets and test results. Keep it quickly retrievable, as you would for e-discovery.

**Supervisory confidentiality:** Classify HKMA correspondence and findings as restricted. Limit access in document systems, and check that collaboration or AI tools do not send confidential supervisory material to third-party services without assessment.
virtualBankNotes: **Business plan:** Expect the HKMA to compare actual performance with the business plan submitted at authorization. Discuss material changes to products, partners or growth before they happen.

**Exit plan:** The digital bank guideline requires an exit plan for an orderly unwind if the business model fails (para 20). Keep it current, because persistent losses or capital pressure will bring it into supervisory discussion.

**Incident visibility:** Technology incidents at a digital bank are visible to customers and the HKMA immediately, so incident reporting is a frequent contact point with the supervisor and a real test of 'no surprises'.

**Securities business:** If the bank distributes investment products as a registered institution, the management accountability and conduct expectations for securities business add another supervisory layer.
pitfalls: **Sharing ratings:** Repeating CAMEL ratings or examination findings to investors, parents or vendors without first consulting the HKMA.
**Late disclosure:** Letting the HKMA learn of a problem from the media or the auditor before hearing it from the bank.
**Privilege waiver:** Producing privileged investigation reports without considering waiver consequences or recording the terms of production.
**Adversarial or informal:** Treating the HKMA like an opposing litigant (adversarial, over-lawyered responses), or the opposite: relying on informal oral understandings with no written record.

glossary.definition: The HKMA's composite supervisory rating covering Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings and Liquidity, assigned on a five-point scale. It sets supervisory intensity and is confidential.
An HKMA inspection of an institution's records, systems and staff, either full-scope or thematic, carried out under the MA's examination powers.
A meeting between the HKMA, the institution and its external auditor to discuss audit and supervisory findings.

A report the MA requires an institution, by notice under s.59(2), to obtain from an MA-approved auditor on matters the MA specifies. It is commonly used to investigate problems or validate remediation.
A person appointed by the MA whose advice an institution is required, under s.52, to seek on the management of its affairs.
A person appointed under s.52 to manage the affairs, business and property of an institution in place of its own management.
The Schedule to the Banking Ordinance listing the grounds on which the MA may revoke an authorization under s.22.

A statutory tribunal, chaired by a person qualified for appointment as a High Court judge, that reviews MA decisions on capital, liquidity and disclosure requirements. It was originally established as the Capital Adequacy Review Tribunal.

title: Recovery & resolution
oneLiner: If the bank fails, contract terms, exit triggers and payout readiness decide whether depositors are paid in an orderly way.
keyPoints: This area covers what happens as a bank moves from stress to failure. It has three layers.

**First, the bank:** its own preparation, a [[recovery plan]] under SPM RE-1 setting out actions it can take itself and, for a digital bank, an [[exit plan]] for an orderly wind-down that does not disrupt customers or the financial system.
**Second, HKMA powers:** its supervisory powers under the Banking Ordinance allow it to give directions or appoint an Advisor or Manager without formal resolution.

**Third, FIRO:** The Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance (Cap. 628) makes the HKMA the resolution authority for banks. Where a bank's failure would threaten financial stability, it can override shareholders, creditors and counterparties.
**Deposit protection:** Alongside these, the Deposit Protection Scheme (Cap. 581) pays insured depositors quickly if a bank is simply liquidated.
**Realistic end-states:** For a small digital bank, a solvent wind-down or liquidation with a DPS payout, rather than bail-in.

conceptMap.caption: For a small digital bank, a solvent wind-down or liquidation with a DPS payout is more realistic than bail-in.

deepDive.heading: Recovery planning under RE-1
deepDive.lede: Start with the escalation ladder. Recovery is led by the bank.
points: **RE-1:** a statutory guideline, revised in 2020.
**Board-owned plan:** It expects a board-owned plan with quantitative and qualitative triggers set above regulatory minimums, credible and tested options, and a communications plan.
**2020 revision:** added triggers such as a rapid fall in profitability and major operational incidents, both relevant to a tech-dependent bank.

deepDive.heading: Supervisory action and liquidation
deepDive.lede: If recovery fails, the MA can act under s.52 of the Banking Ordinance.
points: **Advisor or Manager:** It can direct the bank, appoint an Advisor or, after consulting the Financial Secretary, appoint a Manager to run the business.
**Small banks:** For a small bank these remain the main tools.
**Liquidation:** then proceeds through the court under Cap. 32, with the DPS paying protected depositors up to HK$800,000 each, against a seven-day payout target.

deepDive.heading: LAC, stays and netting
points: **Resolution entities:** [[LAC]] requirements (Cap. 628B) apply only to AIs the HKMA classifies as resolution entities (or their material subsidiaries): in practice the larger banks.
**Classification criteria:** Confirm the current classification criteria with the HKMA.
**Smaller banks:** Two FIRO regimes can still reach a smaller bank.
**Cap. 628C:** The Stay Rules require a [[contractual stay]] term in non-Hong Kong-law financial contracts, recognising the HKMA's power under s.90 to suspend termination rights.
**Cap. 628A:** The Protected Arrangements Regulation governs how set-off, netting and security survive partial transfers.

**Transfer and exit:** They should also support transfer and exit.
**Exit plan:** Align exit-plan triggers with recovery triggers.
**Parent support:** Make the parent's commitment to fund depositor repayment legally binding.

provisions.title: Conditions for initiating resolution
provisions.summary: Resolution may be initiated only if the institution has ceased, or is likely to cease, to be viable, with no reasonable prospect of private-sector action restoring viability. Its non-viability must also pose risks to the stability and effective working of Hong Kong's financial system, including the continued performance of critical financial functions.
provisions.counselNote: For a small digital bank the systemic-risk limb may not be met, which points to insolvency plus a DPS payout rather than FIRO tools. Plan for both paths.

provisions.title: The five stabilization options
provisions.summary: FIRO gives the HKMA, as resolution authority for banking sector entities, five options: transfer to a purchaser, transfer to a bridge institution, transfer to an asset management vehicle, statutory bail-in, and transfer to a temporary public ownership company. FIRO commenced on 7 July 2017.
provisions.counselNote: Transfer-based options only work if contracts, licences and data can follow the business to a new owner. Assignment and novation clauses in key contracts should allow this.

provisions.title: No creditor worse off
provisions.summary: Pre-resolution shareholders and creditors are entitled to compensation if an independent valuation shows they fared worse in resolution than they would have in a hypothetical winding up of the institution.
provisions.counselNote: The comparison is with insolvency, so creditor ranking and set-off positions in a winding up matter even in resolution. Keep the bank's creditor hierarchy analysis current.

provisions.title: MA's powers over a troubled AI
provisions.summary: In defined circumstances, such as an AI likely to be unable to meet its obligations or conducting business in a manner detrimental to depositors, the MA may give directions (s.52(1)(A)) or appoint a Manager to run the AI's affairs, business and property (s.52(1)(C), after consulting the Financial Secretary). The MA may also appoint an Advisor. A Manager's appointment can later be revoked under s.53F.
provisions.counselNote: These are the likeliest intervention tools for a small bank. Check that the insolvency-event definitions in vendor and funding contracts do not treat a s.52 appointment as a termination trigger.

provisions.title: Recovery planning
provisions.summary: A statutory guideline under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance. It requires AIs to maintain board-approved recovery plans with calibrated triggers, stress scenarios, credible recovery options assessed for feasibility and impact, and communication plans, assuming no public support beyond eligibility for HKMA liquidity facilities.
provisions.counselNote: Counsel should check the governance (who can invoke the plan, board approval, annual review) and the legal feasibility of each option, for example whether assets can be sold or a capital raise made quickly.

provisions.instrument: Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks (s.16(10))
provisions.title: Exit plan for a failed business model
provisions.summary: The guideline requires a digital bank applicant to provide an exit plan in case its business model turns out to be unsuccessful, so that the bank can unwind its business operations in an orderly manner without disrupting customers or the financial system. The plan should cover the circumstances that trigger it, the authority to trigger it, the channels for repaying depositors and the source of funding for those payments.
provisions.counselNote: This is a live obligation, not a one-off licensing document. Its triggers should be built into the board's risk appetite and tested alongside the recovery plan.

provisions.title: Deposit Protection Scheme
provisions.summary: Licensed banks are Scheme members unless exempted. Protected deposits are covered up to HK$800,000 per depositor per member bank from 1 October 2024. The Deposit Protection Board targets payout within seven days on a gross basis. Structured deposits, time deposits with an original term over five years, bearer instruments and offshore deposits are not protected.
provisions.counselNote: A digital bank is a Scheme member. Counsel should check product labelling and the DPS membership representations in the app, and the bank's ability to produce depositor data for a fast payout.

provisions.instrument: Financial Institutions (Resolution) (Contractual Recognition of Suspension of Termination Rights - Banking Sector) Rules (Cap. 628C)
provisions.ref: Stay Rules; Code of Practice ST-1
provisions.title: Contractual recognition of resolution stays
provisions.summary: These Rules were made under s.92 of FIRO and came into force on 27 August 2021. Covered entities (Hong Kong-incorporated AIs and certain group companies) must include, in covered financial contracts governed by non-Hong Kong law, a term by which the counterparty agrees to be bound by a suspension of termination rights under s.90 of FIRO (up to two business days). Code of Practice chapter ST-1 explains how the HKMA will exercise its discretions under the Rules.
provisions.counselNote: Inventory any ISDA, GMRA or similar foreign-law contracts and confirm that the stay language or protocol adherence is in place. Technology contracts are not 'financial contracts', so continuity for them depends on drafting.

provisions.title: Operational continuity in resolution
provisions.summary: Issued by the HKMA as resolution authority. It sets expectations for ex-ante arrangements so that critical financial functions and the essential services supporting them, including intra-group and third-party services, can continue during and after resolution. It is read with RA-2 (approach to resolution planning) and CI-1 (core information requirements).
provisions.counselNote: Even where formal resolution planning for the bank is light, OCIR-1 is the best benchmark for resolution-resilient clauses in outsourcing, cloud and intra-group service agreements.

provisions.instrument: Financial Institutions (Resolution) (Loss-absorbing Capacity Requirements - Banking Sector) Rules (Cap. 628B)
provisions.title: Loss-absorbing capacity requirements
provisions.summary: These Rules were made under s.19(1) of FIRO and came into operation on 14 December 2018. They require AIs that the MA classifies as resolution entities, or as material subsidiaries of them, to hold minimum LAC. In practice they reach the larger banks rather than small digital banks; the HKMA decides the classification.
provisions.counselNote: A digital bank is unlikely to be in scope. Confirm this with the HKMA rather than assume it, and keep it under review if the bank grows or is acquired by a larger group.

checklist: **Map critical vendors** (core banking, cloud, payments, card processing, KYC and the parent's shared platforms) and review their termination, suspension and change-of-control triggers. Carve out HKMA directions, s.52 appointments, recovery actions and resolution.

**Negotiate resolution-resilience terms**: continued service while fees are paid, assignment or novation to a purchaser or bridge institution, exit assistance, data return in a usable format, and access to configuration and keys.
**Inventory non-Hong Kong-law financial contracts** and confirm compliance with the Stay Rules, through bespoke clauses or ISDA/ICMA protocol adherence.
**Audit recovery plan governance**: board approval, annual refresh, trigger calibration against the capital and liquidity plan, the escalation chain, and evidence of dry runs.
**Write exit-plan triggers** into the risk appetite statement (for example CET1 runway, losses against plan, missed parent funding milestones) and document who can invoke the plan.
**Make the parent's funding commitment** for depositor repayment and wind-down costs legally enforceable, and test whether it is still credible.
**Verify DPS readiness**: correct protected and non-protected product labelling, membership representations in app and web journeys, and depositor data quality for payout files.
**Prepare an intervention playbook** covering HKMA liaison, board convening, privilege, customer communications, staff retention and preservation of records.
itAngle: **Stack separation:** Operational continuity is an architecture question. Can the bank's stack be separated from the group and handed to a purchaser or bridge institution while the legal owner changes? Shared parent platforms and group-owned cloud tenancies are the usual blockers.

**Exit execution:** Executing an exit plan is a large data-migration and payments project. It needs verified payee details, bulk FPS or transfer repayments, account-closure workflows, mass customer notification and retention of records after the bank ceases business.

**Payout data:** A DPS payout depends on producing accurate depositor-level, aggregated data in the format the Deposit Protection Board prescribes. Treat it as a tested 'single customer view' export, not a one-off script.

**Operational controls:** Continuity clauses only work if the operational controls match: API credentials, encryption keys, admin accounts and data should sit in tenancies the bank controls, with runbooks for vendor exit and handover.
virtualBankNotes: **Exit plan:** The digital bank guideline requires an exit plan covering the triggers, who can trigger it, the depositor repayment channels and the source of funds (para 20). For a loss-making bank this is the most important resolution-related document.
**DPS membership:** As licensed banks, digital banks are DPS members, so protected deposits are covered up to HK$800,000 per depositor.

**Failure paths:** A small digital bank is unlikely to be a LAC resolution entity. Its realistic failure paths are solvent wind-down, a sale or a s.52 Manager, followed by liquidation and a DPS payout.
**Contractual continuity:** Heavy reliance on group platforms and cloud makes contractual continuity critical, even if the HKMA does not require full resolution planning.
pitfalls: **Licensing-stage exit plan:** Treating the exit plan as a licensing-stage document rather than a live plan with calibrated triggers, a named decision-maker and committed funding.

**Insolvency event clauses:** Leaving vendor 'insolvency event' clauses broad enough to catch a regulatory direction, a s.52 Manager or resolution, which hands the vendor a walk-away right at the worst moment.
**Stay Rules scope:** Assuming the Stay Rules protect technology and outsourcing contracts. They target non-Hong Kong-law financial contracts.
**Mislabelled products:** Mislabelling products as deposit-protected (for example structured deposits or long-term time deposits), which creates misrepresentation and DPS compliance issues.

glossary.definition: A bank-owned plan of actions to restore its viability under severe stress without public support beyond normal central bank facilities, with triggers, options and governance (SPM RE-1).
A digital bank's plan for unwinding its business in an orderly way if its business model fails. It covers triggers, who can trigger it, how depositors are repaid and how that repayment is funded.
A stabilization option under which the resolution authority writes down liabilities or converts them into equity to recapitalise a failing institution, without taxpayer funding.
A temporary entity controlled by the resolution authority that takes over critical business from a failing institution so that it can continue until it is sold or wound down.
No creditor worse off: the safeguard by which shareholders and creditors are compensated if resolution leaves them worse off than a hypothetical winding up would have done.

Loss-absorbing capacity: capital and eligible debt that can be written down or converted to absorb losses and recapitalise a bank in resolution. In Hong Kong it is set by Cap. 628B for AIs the HKMA classifies as resolution entities.

A contract term by which a counterparty agrees to be bound by the resolution authority's temporary suspension of its termination rights. It is needed because foreign courts might not otherwise recognise the statutory stay.
Activities, such as deposit-taking and payments, whose sudden discontinuation would be likely to disrupt the financial system or the economy. Their protection is a central objective of resolution.
